Utilizing data from the Pierre Auger Observatory, researchers have analyzed the directional distribution of cosmic rays exceeding 4 EeV. This analysis employs a novel likelihood-based technique applicable to both energy bins and specific energy values, enabling the examination of cosmic-ray anisotropy across a broad spectrum. The results indicate that anisotropes for higher energies within this interval (from 4 to approximately 8 EeV) become progressively more pronounced, peaking near 40% for a particular energy, and simultaneously reaching their maximum for electrons/positrons and other light nuclei. Such substantial anisotropies, particularly those affecting nuclei, are unprecedented and cannot be explained by current propagation models, which typically predict only minor directional variations above the knee energy threshold. These unexpected findings suggest a departure from standard propagation mechanisms at energies above 4 EeV and may point to complex interactions involving the acceleration, selection, or injection of heavy nuclei into the highest-energy cosmic-ray population.

This study investigates the magnitude and direction of elliptic flow ($v_2$) variations, attributed to initial geometric fluctuations in Pb-Pb collisions at the energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV utilizing LHC data. Several analytical methods are employed to examine $e_2$-dependent $v_2$ behavior, exploring correlations across varying centrality levels, with a specific emphasis on the most central collision region. These findings are contrasted against multiple hydrodynamic models to scrutinize the dependence of $v_2$ on initial eccentricity. Additionally, the research addresses the impact of hydrodynamic thermalization and energy loss mechanisms on $e_2$-induced $v_2$ fluctuations within the context of the observed data.

We introduce DisagreementX, a system designed to align data from multiple relational tables that contain nulls and exhibit conflicts. We define a correspondence between two null-hypostatic tables as a collection of disjunctive, first-order logical formulas derived via a top-down algorithm that processes join columns. DisagreementX utilizes these correspondences to construct a reconciled result table by projecting tuples from source inputs and substituting null entries with factually grounded values. We evaluate the system against a industrial-scale dataset comprising 1.1 billion tuples, 1.5 billion nulls, and 1.1 billion join operations across 10 distinct query correspondences. The results demonstrate the practical viability of disjunctive correspondences in handling queries with nulls and discrepancies, supporting up to a 30-fold improvement in efficiency through the identification of disjunctive joins.

The Poisson autoregressive model with exogenous components (PVARXK), introduced by Shibata (1999), functions as a foundational framework for analyzing and forecasting discrete time series. This study proposes a novel class of models termed TV-PARXK, designed specifically to capture trends and seasonal patterns in univariate or multivariate integer time series data. We establish theoretical properties for the proposed model, including representation theorems, necessary and sufficient conditions for stationarity, and impulse response characteristics. Furthermore, we introduce an estimation methodology combining maximum likelihood approaches with an iterative algorithm to compute the Whittle likelihood. The paper's end reveals both theoretical extensions of the TV-PARXK framework and practical application of these concepts through data analysis.

We introduce a novel object representation approach that integrates voxel grids with neural networks to effectively address partial occlusions and robustness to noise. Traditional methods often struggle with issues like sensitivity to noise, problems with occlusion, and high memory consumption; our solution mitigates these challenges while also offering faster sampling speeds and more efficient memory usage compared to existing techniques. To further illustrate the advantages of this method, we present a new synthetic benchmark involving four distinct tasks: object detection, semantic segmentation, pose estimation, and novel view synthesis. In addition to evaluating our approach on synthetic data where it demonstrates clear benefits through improved handling of occlusion and noise across all evaluated tasks, we validated its performance on the real-world ObjectText dataset for novel view synthesis. Finally, we evaluated our method against existing techniques using the REVERIE benchmark for manipulative six-degree-of-freedom pose estimation, finding that Neural Description Fields outperformed comparable approaches in every metric related to pose estimation accuracy.

Building upon an established mapping between the planar XY vertex model and the 6-vertex model evaluated at the 30-degree 3-line configuration, we have redefined a new 8-vertex model 3-line configuration at the Yang-Lee zero critical point. This construct serves as the "Yang-Lee traditional Potts 3-line configuration." Consequently, we have reorganized the planar critical point set for O(N) models—encompassing the 6-vertex (N=1), Ising (N=0), and XY (N=2) systems, along with their non-unitary extensions—into the "Yang-Lee traditional Potts 3-line critical point category." We have further defined a "Yang-Lee traditional Potts 2-line category" to include the critical point sets for 4-line configurations (corresponding to O(N) models at self-dual points) and reclassified the Yang-Lee edge critical point set of the planar Potts 3-line configuration into the "traditional O(N) 2-line category."

In 2009, Talagrand introduced a powerful tool known as the Sudakov-Fernique lemma, which facilitates comparisons between stochastic processes by establishing inequalities for their respective expected supremums over index sets. This lemma has proven to be a foundational element in numerous breakthrough results concerning high-dimensional statistical problems. The current work presents a novel extension of the lemma tailored specifically to the denoised AMP (alternating minimization) process developed by Dobrican in 2016. We further demonstrate Local convexity as a significant property of the TAP free energy function and leverage the post-AMP SF-lemma to analyze various statistical estimators in high dimensions.

Developing tools for rapid and accurate weather forecasting is essential for safeguarding both human health and planetary well-being. Although professional and citizen-steller photometry projects primarily target celestial bodies, their high cadence, long-term consistency, and broad global reach make them valuable for monitoring aerosol optical depth (AOD). We demonstrate an augmented analytical approach that integrates AOD estimates from satellite data and solar total eclipses to calibrate stellar photometry, yielding a method suitable for various sites. Relying on the linear relationship between apparent brightness and actual brightness, this calibration effectively minimizes influences from instrumental variance, differing atmospheric transmission, and stellar position. Using datasets from Zhamkundatschhoi, Georgia—a station operated by the AAVSO with over 20 years of continuous records—we achieved an agreement of less than 0.03 magnitudes for star brightness and 0.02 magnitudes for total sky brightness (fog). These results correspond to precision levels of approximately 7% for AOD and greater than 25% for visibility. Consequently, extensive photometry datasets from aavsos and professional sources can significantly enhance ground-based aerosol assessment systems.

Accurately estimating the six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) spatial pose of an object based on a 2D image feature match with a 3D model is a critical capability in computer vision. This estimation can be achieved by aligning the 3D model until its projected points coincide with the 2D image features, yet this process is often hindered by the presence of multiple solutions that yield identical projections, known as pose ambiguities. To resolve this, we propose "Corresponding Projection Clustering," a strategy that merges several clustering techniques to refine the pose candidate set by filtering out those inconsistent with the actual 2D-3D feature correspondences. Furthermore, to precisely identify the correct pose from these remaining candidates, we introduce a novel deep learning model designed to predict the likelihood of specific 6-DoF poses given a subset of 2D-3D matches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively mitigates pose ambiguity and accurately estimates the final 6-DoF pose.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to solve generalized graphical lasso problems. This tool supports efficient and flexible estimation of the generalized graphical lasso across various covariance functions, enabling users to reconstruct entire families of graphical models. Demonstrating its capabilities, we applied GGLasso to analyze genomic data, assessing how chromatin accessibility changes in response to HIV infection. Our analysis identified several new regions of interest, highlighting the library's practical utility in dynamic research areas.

Configurational sampling constitutes a fundamental challenge in molecular simulations, with advancements in this area directly enabling progress in other critical domains. We introduce a novel application of Langevin dynamics that leverages a specific integrator to effectively sample regions of high probability while simultaneously ensuring adequate visits to regions of low probability. A key feature of this method is its reliance on a time-varying Hamiltonian, which establishes a strong connection between the frequency of visits to any given region and the rate of energy drift within that region. By regulating this energy drift, one can systematically tune the trade-off between sampling accuracy and coverage. This framework is demonstrated through two distinct molecular modeling cases: first, the two-dimensional Lennard-Jones system at criticality, and second, the conformational exploration of n-alkanes in the liquid phase.

The concept of eigenvector centrality has long been utilized to assess the importance of nodes within various types of graphs. However, extending this approach to multilayer networks is complicated by the fact that a node's relevance often depends on the relevance of its neighbors across different layers, a relationship that standard eigenvector methods fail to capture. To resolve this, we propose a new algorithm for multilayer eigenvector centrality that accounts for reliant node significance. We establish a formal framework detailing how nodes in multilayer systems are interrelated and employ numerical experiments to illustrate the applicability of our algorithm. Additionally, we introduce a metric to evaluate the stability of a node's centrality scores against minor perturbations, finding that while the proposed algorithm is effective, it remains vulnerable to certain structural changes. We conclude by discussing potential extensions of this work.

This paper provides a proof of Dirac's formula for the square of the Dirac operator within R-Minkowski spacetimes. Dirac's result is significant because it enables the formulation of first-order field equations derived from the conventional second-order Klein-Gordon equation. The demonstration here utilizes a corresponding generalization known as R-Dirac operator.

This study investigates the surface sealing phenomenon occurring when liquid-covered spheres enter an opposing dry stream of liquid, focusing on the interplay between sphere velocity and wetting conditions. Three distinct phases of behavior are identified: an initial transient phase marked by significant infiltration, followed by a self-sealed regime with minimal leakage, and finally a leak-dominated regime where infiltration rates escalate with increasing speed. The transition from the self-sealed state to leakage dominance is triggered when inertial forces surpass surface tension, quantified via a Froude number threshold dependent on the contact angle. Observations reveal that lower surface tension hysteresis and higher sphere velocities promote the development of a self-sealed state. To explain these dynamics, a force balance model accounting for surface tension, inertia, and viscosity is presented, demonstrating strong alignment with experimental leakage data. Furthermore, a new theoretical model for the self-sealed state, based on radial momentum balance, accurately predicts the radial distribution of axial velocity within the reformed meniscus.

The magnetic ordering observed in CuFe$_{2}$S$_{3}$ (cubanite) serves as a test case for theories predicting orbital-selective Mott physics. Recent work by Li et al. offers a Hubbard-model explanation that aligns well with available experimental data. This test reveals that cubanite features a narrow, oxygen-2p orbital-selective band associated with the Fe$^{3+}$ ion, which is positioned approximately 1 eV above the non-bonding ground-state band. While the orbital-selective behavior of this 2p band accounts for certain properties, it fails to replicate the compound's charge-carrier mass or magnetic ordering temperature. Consequently, these characteristics indicate strong and significant electron-electron correlations within the orbitally degenerate 3d shell.

The development of semiconductor materials, such as GaAs, has significantly advanced the practical use of Rabi oscillations, a phenomenon characterized by the periodic inversion of a two-level system's state through resonant light-matter interaction. However, natural two-level systems face inherent constraints, including thermal equilibrium limitations and spectral diffusion, which can hinder the utility of Rabi oscillations. This study investigates the impact of a dark exciton, a two-level entity defined by the coupling between an exciton and a dark state, on observed Rabi oscillations. Findings reveal that, under specific conditions, dark excitons can facilitate the massive Rabi oscillations of a two-level system. These results are particularly promising as they overcome several traditional barriers, including the establishment of thermal non-equilibrium, spectral diffusion, and the necessity for high magnetic fields. Achieving this breakthrough relies on synchronizing the polarization of a laser beam with that of an exciton, thereby triggering strong light-matter coupling between a bright and dark pair state. Furthermore, the research explores various influencing factors, such as laser detuning, coupling strength, and exciton-phonon interaction, and offers a potential pathway to realize Rabi oscillations within a dark two-level system by utilizing dark exciton massiveness via semiconductor material engineering.

Recent progress in material science has prominently featured novel electronic states hosted within gaps, such as those at locations with high symmetry. Among these, Dirac states—characterized by two crossed bands crossing linearly and forming a "Dirac cone"—are notably distinct. These crossings often involve non-trivial crystalline symmetries, leading to protection within gaps that are unavailability for conventional parabolic crossings. The current research introduces a Ti-based 2D metallic perovskite structure belonging to the P2mm (non-symorphic rectangular) space group. Analysis via first-principles calculations reveals that the vertical mirror symmetry of this material induces linear band crossings between a pair of Dirac fermions situated at distinct points on the Fermi surface within the Brillouin zone. Uniquely, the positions of these intersections can be adjusted by altering the Ti–cation bond length. Specifically, varying the Ti 3d orbital overlap across different cations results in a shift of the intersections along the k-direction perpendicular to the plane. The study demonstrates that the intersections remain robust against interactions and thermal fluctuations. The findings presented herein contribute to the understanding of non-symmetry structures and possess potential applications in designing novel electronic materials.

Catalyzing a traveling light's mode by measuring a local probe mode containing a specific quantum state is an effective method for generating remarkable hybrid optical states. This paper examines the effect of measuring an Fock state $|n\rangle$ in a local probe mode on a signal mode initially prepared in a coherent state $\alpha$. When the measurement outcome indicates that $n$ photons were successfully recorded, the signal mode transforms into what we term a single-photon facilitated coherent state (SPFCS). The SPFCS is shown to be non-classical, exhibiting large violations of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for optical correlations, along with strong non-Gaussian characteristics. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the SPFCS's geometric features through its phase-space trajectories and quantum ellipticity.

Using the Newman-Penrose formalism, this study investigates the geometric characteristics of bivectors constructed from complex self-dual and anti-self-dual expansion-free null dyads. We demonstrate that a real electromagnetic field tensor corresponds to the sum of a specific self-dual and a specific anti-self-dual bivector, whereas a (self-conjugate) Weyl tensor represents a specific linear combination of four distinct self-dual bivectors. By exploring the decomposition of a real EM tensor into self-dual and anti-self-dual components, we derive expressions for the field strength invariants. Furthermore, through the factorization of self-dual bivectors into simple null forms, we establish a direct link between the principal null directions of the Weyl tensor and the metric of this specific self-dual matrix. Knowledge of the EM invariants allows for the determination of the factorized self-dual form, which in turn yields the induced metric on the complex projective space formed by the EM field's principal null directions. Finally, given a spin coefficient-dependent set of Newman-Penrose coefficients, we construct a specific self-dual form in terms of the connection coefficients of the torsion-free affine structure defining the complex projective structure on Minkowski space.

This research examines a method for performing integer programming across an extensive range of entire functions, utilizing this approach to model complex, non-linear relationships within the theoretical chemistry of polymer physics. Specifically, the Ryberg model—which originally employed exponential and polynomial terms to determine a novel kind of "random" polymer theory based on length and connectivity—was re-derived using this new integer programming framework. Remarkably, the original theory's considerable mathematical sophistication could be reconstructed solely from simple molecular isomers defined by length and topology without exponential or polynomial variables. Although inputs were represented purely in terms of length and topology, the method inherently generates new monomer chemical interactions that correspond to various polymers. Finally, the paper investigates how this integer programming-based scaling law applies to other systems, including new previously unmodeled monomer chemistries that depend on their specific arrangement of chemical bonds.

Delineating high-risk esophageal lesions is a standard step in diagnosing and treating esophageal disorders. Manual segmentation by radiologists remains a standard practice, yet it is often hindered by the difficulty in clearly distinguishing neoplastic tissue from surrounding structures in CT images. While Deep Learning (DL) techniques have shown promise in segmenting various organ pathologies, their application to esophageal lesion segmentation continues to face challenges. To address this, we introduce DDAUnet, a novel Deep Learning framework built upon the U-Net architecture. This model incorporates dilated dense convolution blocks to enhance the spatial resolution of skipped connections in the encoder and employs a focus mechanism within the decoder to aid in precisely delineating lesion boundaries. We evaluated DDAUnet using 90 contrast-enhanced axial CT scans from 45 patients showing malignant or high-grade benign lesions. Our experiments demonstrate that DDAUnet significantly outperforms the standard U-Net baseline. The model was evaluated using multiple metrics, including the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), 90th percentile Hausdorff Distance ($HD_{90}$), and 90th percentile surface distance ($90\%$ SD). Blending English with native languages constitutes code switching, a phenomenon prevalent in many multilingual societies. Although existing English-centered Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools can often manage this input, they frequently neglect the nuanced obstacles and driving forces behind such switching. This paper defines and addresses five specific switching barriers and motivators within NLP frameworks: character, word, phrase, sentence, and semantic switching. Furthermore, we introduce a unified, probabilistic representation tailored to switching barriers that captures a switching strand—a single continuous sequence of switched units—throughout a text. Distinct from prior work, our approach is dynamic; it infers switch rates by calculating the probability of switching versus not switching, offering insights into the underlying motivations. Finally, we present "SwitchBerts," an innovative static and dynamic code switching barrier-aware model. Evaluations using both datasets and real-world news articles demonstrate SwitchBerts's efficacy in identifying and locating switching units with superior precision, recall, and F1 scores compared to current baselines.

Automatic image description models are typically evaluated using automatic metrics such as BLEU, which measure the similarity between generated references and human references. However, relying exclusively on these multiple generated references often fails to accurately reflect actual image semantic content. This study proposes a new approach to construct a human reference by integrating multiple generated references against a specific set of criteria. We use this new "all-in-one" reference to assess traditional metrics for evaluating automatic image descriptions. Through experiments, we demonstrate that re-evaluating these metrics with our proposed "all-in-one" reference yields more appropriate outcomes.

Tantalum pentoxide (Ta$_2$O$_5$) serves as a leading dielectric in advanced gate stacks for metal-oxide-semiconductors and may function as an ionic solid with potential relevance to interplanetary spacecraft. However, despite extensive research, its ground-state crystal configuration remains elusive. This study addresses that uncertainty by employing advanced density functional theory (DFT) calculations and a molecular dynamics (MD) approach. Systematically examining 250 plausible structural candidates, we identified 11 configurations featuring exceptional stability. Notably, a structure we designate "Ta-O-1" emerged as the most stable arrangement according to DFT principles. Consequently, "Ta-O-1" was selected for extensive molecular crystal Monte Carlo simulations, which successfully matched experimental diffraction data regarding both Bragg peaks and diffuse scattering patterns. Our analysis confirms that "Ta-O-1" comprises discrete Ta$_2$O$_5$ molecular units arranged in a triclinic lattice. We further determined that reorientational motions of these molecules are responsible for the dielectric relaxation observed in low-frequency dielectric measurements. Given its superior thermodynamic stability compared to existing theoretical models, "Ta-O-1" is proposed as the genuine base state of tantalum pentoxide.

U.S. political misinformation poses a significant risk to the nation's social cohesion and democratic processes. While prior research has examined the characteristics of misinformation itself, there is a notable absence of study regarding how Reddit users interact with and spread these falsehoods. To address this gap, we analyze a dataset containing 1.3 million unique posts and 23 million comments from r/politics between 2017 and 2019. We identify "Big Geographic Arrangements" (BigGAs)—visualizations depicting a U.S. map where state sizes reflect voter turnout rather than land area—as a primary source of widespread political misinformation within the subreddit. Although BigGAs were present in nearly every week during the study period, accounting for 26\% of all visual shares, they constituted only 3.8\% of total misinformation. Paradoxically, their low volume correlates with their high impact; users cited BigGAs more frequently than any other misinformation type, and they generated the most replies despite being shared less often. We argue that BigGAs functioned as a potent "social conversation starter" by generating immediate, visceral reactions regarding the apparent discrepancy between Texas and California landmasses, even though accurately interpreting the data required understanding the nuance of "vote casting" versus "voter participation." Ultimately, BigGAs exemplify how certain misinformation achieves disproportionate influence not necessarily through ubiquity, but by triggering strong emotional engagement.

Human-robot collaboration is increasingly common in industrial settings, with robots learning new tasks through demonstration. While visual and tactile methods of demonstration are well-established, this study shows that embedding audio guidance significantly improves a robot's ability to understand and replicate complex manipulation jobs. We propose a novel dataset capturing humans teaching robotic arms via integrated audio instructions, including corresponding visual and force-torque data to ensure audio relevance. Analysis of this dataset highlights distinct acoustic signatures in successful demonstrations and a strong correlation between these patterns and demonstration quality. We further argue that integrating audio guidance benefits both the practical execution of tasks and the robot learning process itself.

We introduce an alternative metric for the group of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms (D), derived from the standard one on R via their action, such that the corresponding Euler-Poincarre equation models a constant curvature Hamiltonian system. This framework yields a formulation of the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations as a constant curvature theory. By integrating the concept of constant curvature with our alternative metric, we establish a new classification for topologically constant curvature theories. Specifically, we prove it is impossible for 3D Euler, Kelvin-Helmholtz, and Saint-Venant hydrodynamic models to be constant curvature systems under this definition. Additionally, we apply the alternative metric to 3D Euler and 3D Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) dynamics to study geodesic complexity. Our analysis of both the 3D Euler and 3D KdV equations reveals that all minimizers of geodesic complexity possess either Eulerian or point support vorticities.

To address the surge in conversational AI applications, we have established a comprehensive, open evaluation platform built upon the BotEval framework. This system streamlines the creation of conversational evaluations by providing tools to develop interactive tasks, robust assessment methodologies, and high-quality dialogue models. Specifically, we have created a flexible framework for constructing dialogue assessment benchmarks, illustrating its application with a new benchmark featuring reading comprehension questions derived from Wikipedia abstracts. Furthermore, we have implemented several hands-on demonstrations, including one utilizing sentence semantic similarity to gauge conversational relevance and another for evaluating task-oriented dialogue based on database query success. In response to the growing demand for conversational agents capable of generating open-domain dialogue, we also established a suite of top-tier, large-scale dialogue models. By unifying our created resources and empirical studies into a single initiative, we hope to advance future research in conversational AI.

Recommendation systems are increasingly facing data sparsity and sparseness, which hampers their ability to provide accurate suggestions. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) framework. The proposed approach enhances a user's preference modeling by integrating and leveraging information from several sparse domains. Specifically, the framework consists of three primary modules: First, it develops an Aspect-Based Social Attention (ABSA) module to extract and model thematic preferences from social interaction data. Second, it implements a Cross-Domain Interaction (CDI) module designed to capture connections between different sparse domains through learned embedding interactions. Finally, the framework employs a Multi-Sparse-Domain Co-Preferential Learning (MSD-CP) module to synthesize these enriched, cross-domain, and aspect-aware representations for more precise recommendations. Experiments conducted across five diverse datasets validate the proposed method's superiority over current state-of-the-art techniques.

Although Hypatia is currently restricted to convex conic domains, our extension of the package enables the modeling of various non-convex optimizations involving single and bi-linear cones, which we term "organic conics," and we demonstrate this capability using an representative implementation in Julia. By leveraging the CVXPY interface, we transformed a Julia script utilizing organic conic constraints into an equivalent version compatible with Hypatia. Our findings reveal that this translation approach can automate a substantial portion of the coding necessary to build custom conic formulations. Furthermore, our tests indicate that optimization results generated by the Hypatia interface closely mirror those from the original CVXPY version.

Although MRI quality assurance (QA) is critical for ensuring high clinical standards, widespread adoption has been hindered by the inconvenience and expense of routine testing. Recent initiatives have sought to bypass manual checks by using deep learning to identify QA defects from MRI images, yet these models often require extensive labeling across numerous device types and sequences. This paper introduces a novel hypothesis: effective MRI QA defects detection can be achieved with minimal labeling by treating it as a generative adversarial network (GAN) image-to-image translation task. Instead of producing detailed segmentations, the model generates "masked" copies of input images where regions of defects appear as distortions. We rename this approach I2D (Image-to-Defect). As the adoption rate of electric vehicles (EVs) continues to rise, the expanding number of privately owned units significantly influences power system resilience. This study introduces a novel multi-agent optimization framework designed to address the evasive behaviors of private EV drivers during extreme weather events characterized by both adverse conditions and grid disruptions. Within this structure, a "cloud" agent represents the distribution network operator, managing a collection of "micro" EV agents. The cloud agent employs reinforcement learning to anticipate private agents' unobservable traits, such as risk tolerance and information asymmetry, while also incorporating a discrete choice model grounded in stochastic utility theory to further refine these behavioral predictions. Disruptions to the power grid trigger cascading failures, resulting in widespread outages, financial losses, and social costs. Consequently, enhancing network resilience is vital for mitigating these impacts. By integrating private EV agent behavior into optimization strategies, the research demonstrates an improvement in the operator's ability to maintain service and allocate resources effectively during crises. Ultimately, the proposed method offers network operators a robust tool for bolstering resilience against weather-related disruptions, which are increasingly common and damaging.

This paper proposes a new approach to schedule agent meetings via an agent-to-agent communication protocol. This method is designed to accommodate multiple concurrent meetings and agents, allowing participants to express their availability and preferences through a series of exchanges. The suggested model functions as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) where each participant aims to maximize their individual utility. This "selfish" behavior often leads to suboptimal collective outcomes, known as the social welfare problem. To address this, the authors introduce a solution based on a meeting schedule reward mechanism that incentivizes better overall results. Unlike previous approaches requiring a centralized reward calculator, this method derives the incentive directly from the traffic data of the agents themselves. The effectiveness of this decentralized algorithm was validated through simulations comparing it to a baseline MDP and a recurrency-based strategy.

Sloshing-Sagnac interferometers function as ultra-sensitive accelerometers capable of detecting picometer-level displacements at megahertz frequencies, making them promising candidates for next-generation, high-grain accelerometers in gravitational wave detectors. We examine an XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol designed for large-scale networks involving numerous APs within an XL-MIMO system sharing a single baseband processing unit. In this framework, the protocol grants transmission rights only to APs whose visibility areas do not intersect with those of other active transmitters. While increasing system throughput is a common advantage of such protocols, our analysis reveals a counterintuitive outcome: the total achievable throughput may actually decrease compared to a scenario without these non-intersection constraints. We introduce a novel framework for 3D facial reconstruction and expression recognition designed to handle diverse facial structures and dynamic changes in appearance. This framework integrates two key modules: a Self-aligned Dual (SAD) reconstruction network and an Appearance transformation (AT) module. The core SAD reconstruction network splits the prediction process into two phases: first, a cross-modal network converts cross-facial expression variations into 3D landmarks, and second, two unimodal networks handle the conversion of cross-facial structure variations into 3D landmarks. The AT module bridges the gap between the two networks by integrating cross-facial appearance changes into the 3D landmarks. Experiments show that our framework outperforms current methods in both 3D face landmarking and facial expression recognition.

Global atmospheric circulations on exoplanets are shaped by a balance of thermal forcing, Coriolis effects, and friction. This study examines how these factors drive circulation patterns in zero-dimensional energy balance models paired with simplified two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic dynamics. The models simulate heating at the day-side and cooling at the night-side of tidally locked planets orbiting various stars. A prominent pressure gradient forms due to the temperature difference between the sub-stellar and anti-stellar points, generating an eastward jet driven by the planet's thermal forcing relative to the thermal forcing ratio. Distinct regimes emerge based on the interplay of stellar forcing and the oblateness coefficient: strong forcing or low oblateness yields eastward jets with multiple meanders resembling geostrophic turbulence, while weak forcing or high oblateness produces strong super-rotational jets. Notably, the transition from cyclostrophic geostrophic stability occurs when forcing is weak or oblateness is high. The study offers insights into atmospheric dynamics across different planetary radii and provides a framework for analyzing atmospheric circulation in other exoplanetary systems.

Deep neural networks have advanced significantly, yet their improvement rates have slowed recently. While prior research has mostly focused on developing new architectures or employing larger static batches, this work argues for the pivotal role of dynamic learning rates image-wide. We introduce a method that adjusts these rates in real-time, allowing the model to evolve throughout training. Our approach demonstrates that dynamic learning can scale to the Imagenet dataset and beyond, achieving performance comparable to the best static models. Furthermore, our strategy proves particularly advantageous when scaling to larger datasets and more complex models.

The performance of silicon-based quantum computers is significantly influenced by spin–orbit interactions arising from donor dopants, which enable all configurations to exist and facilitate gate completion. However, calculating these configuration interactions requires handling the complex band structures of silicon. This computational challenge has been addressed through "n-valley" effective Hamiltonians, yet selecting optimal parameters remains difficult. We present a novel approach to derive these parameters specifically for pairs of donor states, ensuring that the target $|00\rangle$ and $|11\rangle$ quantum states become completely decoupled from all other orthogonal states via exact numerical integration. We implemented this method to determine multi-donor interaction parameters, identifying a set that successfully reproduces the CI evolution. Using these parameters, we simulated CI outcomes with near-complete accuracy, particularly for deep donor impurities where effects are most pronounced.

We analyze the transport properties of a two-dimensional topological insulator, specifically HgTe, featuring a negative mass and an associated Dirac point. By introducing a "quantum trench" defined as two parallel grooves etched into the sample, we observe that when the grooves are sufficiently narrow, the system's effective behavior is described by a one-dimensional Dirac equation. Under these conditions, only two propagating modes emerge, characterized by a linearly dispersing "rim" within the sample's bulk band structure. We further examine how charged impurities and magnetic fields influence this geometry; notably, the resulting Hofstadter spectrum transforms into a Dirac delta function when projected onto the trench's Dirac Hamiltonian. Finally, utilizing the transfer matrix method, we calculate the transmission characteristics across various impurity and defect configurations, including point defects, individual and interacting defects, and defects situated at the trench boundaries.

Dynamic Time Division Duplexing (TDD) allows user equipment to utilize uplink and downlink radio resources based on current traffic demands, a key enabler for the next-generation 5G network. Within this framework, the optimal transmission interval, known as the time slot duration, is critical for performance. This study models the slot duration selection as a non-cooperative game to analyze the resulting allocation strategies. The findings reveal that the optimal allocation exhibits a distinct threshold characteristic: users with channel gain exceeding a specific limit choose longer slots, whereas those below it select shorter ones. Furthermore, the optimal allocation is derived as a function of system parameters, including the number of active users, their distribution, average channel strength, and total base station capacity. Numerical simulations confirm that this game-theoretic allocation model significantly enhances network-wide sum-rate performance compared to both fixed allocations and existing dynamic methods.

This study introduces a gradient-constrained (GC) optimization approach utilizing structured Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs), where state derivatives are bounded according to specific task requirements. We demonstrate that integrating these constraints into an energy-minimization framework yields superior generalization compared to standard gradient-flow optimization, even when parameterized gradients contain errors. Our analysis provides theoretical bounds for parameter learning under imperfect gradient estimation and supports this theory with empirical data from experiments on both classification and regression tasks.

To address this, we propose an asymmetric multi-agent framework designed to identify and remove untrustworthy samples. We evaluate the approach on standard classification tasks and demonstrate that the method effectively reduces error rates for impostor data. Additionally, we analyze various configuration factors, including the out-of-distribution dataset used for agent training, the specific enrichment strategy, and the optimal number of in- and out-of-distribution samples.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) addresses the challenge of identifying the appropriate meaning of words based on their specific context. Since many entries for a single word are distributed across various real-world scenarios, effective WSD must integrate not only rich contextual information but also extralinguistic knowledge, such as definitions and synonyms. This paper introduces a simple yet effective method for word sense disambiguation that enhances a basic contextual approach by incorporating context-independent glosses. Our results on two standard datasets demonstrate that this proposed method significantly improves upon a baseline contextual model.

The proposed method was rigorously evaluated on the widely recognized Spider benchmark text-to-SQL dataset. The evaluation results demonstrate superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methodologies.

Differential confidentiality (DP) has become the standard for ensuring privacy when querying databases. Extending this guarantee to graphs is challenging due to the interconnected nature of entities, where an individual's presence often depends on their relationships with others. We analyze these proposals from the perspective of data publishers seeking to safeguard individual privacy while providing query services to consumers. These models face significant hurdles, including fundamental conflicts between related privacy guarantees, compatibility with standard mechanisms, and the difficulty of defining an entity's existence in a networked context. In our survey, we categorize these challenges, explore potential resolutions, and highlight open issues regarding the deployment of confidentiality on graphs.

Excluding the effect of photon recoil on laser cooling theory is a standard practice, as it typically has a negligible influence on spectral line shapes in conventional single-beam absorption spectroscopy with high-power lasers. Users of Google Web Search may unknowingly disregard a vast amount of information due to algorithmic personalization. To demonstrate this effect and quantify its scope, we conducted controlled experiments on 50 carefully selected queries representing diverse topics. By comparing search results with and without personalized customization, we measured the "Jaccard similarity" between result sets. High-intensity lepton beams are fundamental to the advancement of physics, yet current limitations in proton acceleration efficiency hinder the production of more energetic options. Since directly scaling proton masses to TeV levels is not currently viable, we propose a promising path forward by accelerating single charges of approximately $2000\text{ GeV}$ in the 2000 GeV mass range. This proposal envisions a muon-ion composite beam, specifically a bound state of an electron and a proton, with a total mass of approximately 2000 GeV. By leveraging the muon charge's high velocity gain, we can leverage existing, well-develop acceleration technologies to achieve TeV-scale operations. This approach promises to deliver high-energy collisions that are unattainable with current generations of accelerators, thereby enabling physics investigations at energy frontiers previously inaccessible.

T2-weighted (T2w) 3D MRI is a standard procedure for assessing thoracic and abdominal pathology. Although turbo spin-echo (TSE) sequences are typically used for these scans, applications involving large diaphragmatic movement ranges often require adjusting for respiration. Standard methods offer only two acquisition modes: free breathing or breath holding. However, neither optimally addresses significant motion; free breathing results in image degradation due to blurring, while breath holding causes artifacts when actual patient movement exceeds the modeled range. To address this, we developed a free breathing, motion-adjusted technique for RARE T2w 3D MRI in the projection domain. This method dynamically alters the k-t space trajectory to align with a prescribed respiratory pattern, enabling flexible free-breathing scans. Validation was conducted on phantom models with controlled motion and on both healthy and diseased patients. A motion-correction post-processing algorithm was applied to demonstrate reduced blurring and improved visual quality compared to conventional free-breathing acquisitions. Subject evaluations by two radiologists confirmed that the motion-adjusted approach offers superior diagnostic value over the standard free-breathing method.

Although automated metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, and WER are standard for evaluating generative tasks such as text summarization and speech recognition, a critical question remains: do these metrics truly differentiate meaningful model improvements? To address this, we introduce Precise Paired-Permutation Examination (PPEx), a statistically rigorous method that pairs-permutation tests the null hypothesis of no difference under bootstrap resampling. Unlike traditional approaches limited to a fixed confidence level, PPEx determines the exact confidence with which a specific result was achieved. We evaluate 15 pairwise comparisons across three domains—synthetic data, real-world scenarios, and human evaluations—demonstrating that PPEx provides more informative insights than traditional fixed confidence intervals.

This study introduces a comprehensive dataset encompassing five critical dimensions of the U.S. for-hire cargo shipping industry between 1966 and 1994: waterborne freight ton-miles, expenditures on new and used shipping assets, scrap values, total cargo shipping costs, and costs allocated specifically to new construction. Collaborating with the Federal Reserve Board, we merge historical NAICS-based estimates from 1966–1994 with pre-war accounting records to form a continuous 29-year dataset. Complementing this, we develop an indexing methodology utilizing scrap and used sale prices to quantify capital investment. Finally, we establish these physical and price indices against existing sector-wide measures, ensuring their integration into broader economic analyses.

Triangulations of a surface are traditionally classified up to isotopy using the theory of splitting and flipping. For these fabric spaces, a corresponding splitting theory and associated divergence metrics are established. It is demonstrated that distinct initial structures yield sufficiently large metric values to guarantee the existence of structures isomorphic to one another. This proof strategy relies on constructing a specific flow across the space of configurations and analyzing the construction of structures along these trajectories.

Although various studies have utilized deep learning to analyze financial data, the specific applications for predicting stock prices remain challenging. This paper introduces a methodology combining the BERT model with stock textual information and a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to forecast stock prices. BERT effectively processes the language aspects of financial data, while the GGAN generates missing values for unstructured numerical reports, integrating them with standard stocks metrics for prediction. When applied to the Korean stock market, the proposed approach demonstrated higher accuracy compared to existing traditional and textual-based prediction methods.

Four specific Beyond Standard Model scenarios are analyzed: the Two-Higgs Doublet Model (both Type-II and the approximation where one mass is negligible), an extension with three Higgs doublets, and both an extension with one extra singlet and mixing. For each model, the study details how parameters influence production cross-sections. Particular attention is given to the physical meaning of coupling constants and their impact on measurable quantities. Furthermore, the work investigates how various effects modify the standard model limit of Higgs interactions. Based on projections for sensitivity at the High-Luminosity LHC and the Future Circular Collider, the research identifies the conditions under which these new physics structures can be discovered and characterized.

The direction-dependent disparity in forces acting on objects moving through granular materials is widely recognized as a key driver of patterns like those found in conical assemblies. We employ both dry and liquid-bound monosized spherical grains to measure the drag forces on cylinders moving at varying angles. Our findings reveal that oblique drag exhibits strong material dependence: in fluid-grains systems, it aligns with the sum of direction-averaged drag perpendicular and parallel to the flow, indicating material independence. Conversely, dry grains behave dependently on material properties. We attribute this divergence to the distinct mechanisms governing force transmission in each medium—specifically, how they handle energy dissipation and mechanical stability.

Depth-aware methods for flow estimation offer a significant advantage over standard approaches by incorporating an extra dimension of information. Nevertheless, collecting labeled datasets containing both flow and depth data is resource-intensive and difficult to achieve. Depth inference can automatically generate such depth information for flow training datasets, though it introduces certain challenges. Experiments conducted on the challenging and real-world KITTI dataset demonstrate that this method effectively combines performance in both flow and depth tasks using only one dataset.

The proposed solution demonstrates that an RNN can effectively categorize videos containing cats, highlighting potential applications in areas like surveillance and search-and-rescue missions. Additionally, since the RNN operates spikingly, it offers substantial energy savings and high-speed processing capabilities.

This paper presents a time-domain expanded source (ES) method designed to mitigate boundary effects in seismic reflection data. The approach interprets reflection data from finite domains by integrating virtual sources within the computational domain alongside the physical sources. These virtual sources generate upward-propagating waves that mimic those produced by real downward-propagating sources but reflected off the domain's lower edge. By combining Green's functions derived from mixed initial and boundary conditions with those from equivalent infinite-domain scenarios, we formulate a reflection Green's function suitable for use in reflection seismometry. Substituting the standard infinite-domain reflection Green's function with this new version transforms reflection imaging objectives into expansion source objectives. Numerical tests demonstrate that this method successfully minimizes artifacts caused by artificial boundaries.

This research examines the impact of interspecific competition on population persistence within a two-species extension of the two-map chaotic territorial voter model featuring colonization-competition balance. In this framework, a superior map yields a global attractor characterized by its dominant presence, while the second map exists only as a coexisting chaotic attractor. Numerical analysis reveals that even when both maps share the same topological structure—indicating complex, co-plausible dynamics—populations of second competitors can still face elimination. Furthermore, varying the dimensionality of the dominant map's attractor directly influences the long-term stability and distribution densities of second map populations. This study offers a novel numerical demonstration that colonization-competition dynamics can drive species extinction despite biological and dynamic complexity sufficient for theoretical coexistence.

In data-centric scenarios where power transmission is equally vital, coexisting D2D communications struggle due to significant interference from both wireless power transfer and intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS). To address this, we propose a novel IRS-coordinated D2D framework that integrates wireless charging and smart building blocks. This design enables each block to harvest energy and deliver it wirelessly to matched receivers, while the IRS dynamically optimizes both power and data rates through coordinated reflection. We formulate a non-concave, coupled optimization problem aimed at maximizing the minimum user-coordinated D2D data rate within this infrastructure. By applying a successive convex approximation method, we transform the problem into a series of convex sub-problems solvable via semidefinite relaxation and iterative variable updates. The resulting algorithm guarantees convergence to at least a locally optimal configuration. Extensive simulations validate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

Displacement measurements, which are highly sensitive to minute changes, serve as a critical component in numerous industrial applications. Among the various techniques available, Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) stands out for its ability to accurately determine normal displacements at specific points. To capture both the location and magnitude of defects, an approach combining LDV with image processing was developed. This method relies on an automated system that roams a predefined area to identify anomalies, utilizing LDV to verify findings after potential issues are flagged by image analysis. To effectively operate this system, it is essential to manage the LDV instrument remotely and efficiently log the data's spatial coordinates and values. Consequently, this study proposes a communication protocol designed for single-point LDV applications. Implemented within a standard Ethernet infrastructure, the new protocol adheres to the Modbus TCP standard to ensure broad compatibility. The resulting framework is modular, allowing for future integrations, and has been validated through experimental results.

Programmable spatial light modulators (PSLMs) are emerging as a transformative innovation for Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs), promising to turn these instruments into adaptable systems. We present the comprehensive design, fabrication methodology, and performance validation of this circular PSLM. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by utilizing the device within a TEM to correct spherical aberration, successfully producing images of gold nanoparticles with dimensions as small as 2 nm.

We discovered that nuclei cease migrating at approximately 4 days post-fertilization (dpf), a stage at which the photoreceptor layer begins to form. The reliability of polarized intensity and total magnetic field strength relies on the accuracy of linearly and circularly intensity data, especially in solar regions where these values are inherently low. Fluctuations in the retrieval of circular intensity, which are linked to the orientation angle's uncertainty, frequently introduce spurious "kinks" in the calculated P.I. and B-values. Although current inversion techniques have largely eliminated the bias in linearly polarized intensity, the circular intensity remains prone to errors, necessitating revised strategies to eliminate this residual bias and enhance the quality of vector magnetic field analyses.

Variational Monte Carlo methods utilizing neural networks have become a leading approach for investigating the sign dilemma associated with fermionic wavefunction evaluation. This issue stems from the potentially complex-valued result of neural network formulations and the consequent complex-valued products required to determine their Monte Carlo weights. Such operations are inherently computation-intensive. Furthermore, in scenarios involving a significant sign problem—where these weights exhibit largely negative values—numerical inaccuracies often cause these weights to approach zero artificially, causing collapse of sampling efficiency. To address this, we propose a novel architecture featuring a complex-valued neural network composed of two synchronized real-valued networks. This design ensures that calculations of local weight amplitudes and phases occur independently, thereby enhancing computational speed, numerical stability, and accuracy while eliminating both stochastic and system-induced barriers to resolving the sign problem. Our hypothesis is that maintaining continuity in the combined amplitude and phase approximations prevents this efficiency collapse, a premise we validate through tests using our proposed model for various architectures.

Humans excel at transferring knowledge across domains without relying on labels, a capability that current neural models struggle to match. This paper introduces Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Task Learning (RAMTL), an unsupervised framework designed to boost cross-task generalization. In RAMTL, retrieval suggestions drawn from external, unlabeled data guide interactions among tasks. We evaluate our approach on eight binary classification problems within a multi-task setting, comparing its performance against a strong baseline that uses shared parameterizations. Results indicate that RAMTL achieves an average improvement of 3.3% in F1 scores, with gains reaching up to 5.7% on specific tasks. Additionally, analyses of transfer learning and suggestions derived from the corpus support the model's ability to generalize effectively.

This study introduces a robust hyperparameter tuning methodology designed to establish differential privacy (DP) parameters for deep learning models. While prior research has largely fixed these parameters or treated them as non-critical, we argue that optimizing DP settings alongside other hyperparameters is essential for achieving high model accuracy while preserving security. We address the inherent difficulty of this task: because hyperparameter choices influence data structure and thus privacy requirements, and because rigorous hyperparameter search often necessitates splitting training data into held-out sets—violating DP constraints—a conflict arises. To resolve this, we propose a framework where hyperparameter candidates are evaluated exclusively on subsets of the training data. This approach avoids data splitting violations by ensuring all search processes remain within the DP context, requiring only a single budget allocation for the entire search. Although search steps remain approximate, we demonstrate that this strategy effectively identifies top-performing hyperparameters. Empirical results confirm that our tuned models attain nearly identical privacy levels with only a marginal increase in cost compared to fixed parameters, yet they deliver significantly higher accuracy under those secure constraints.

The distribution of stellar populations across the Milky Way disk is governed by processes involving both stellar feedback and mixing, which can be investigated through the "remaining abundances" method. This technique utilizes the correlation between the yields of chemical elements produced in stellar remnants and those retained within the interstellar medium to establish chemical mapping frameworks. Such mappings reveal distinct trends in disk stellar populations that standard yield-based models often obscure. Employing the two-Procedure Model (2PM)—which accounts for the fact that only specific processes occur within certain regimes—we demonstrate that the 2PM successfully reproduces the chemical evolution histories of stellar samples drawn from the Apache Asteroid Lexicon (APOGEE) database. Furthermore, our results indicate that the 2PM provides a superior fit for these data compared to conventional chemical evolution models. We attribute this improvement to the 2PM's ability to model the specific feedback mechanisms responsible for the production and retention of chemical elements.

This study examines the dissemination patterns of China's COVID-19 related digital rumors, analyzing the characteristics of rumor sources, content, and transmission pathways. The research focuses on the effect of personal attributes—such as demographics, social networks, and trustworthiness—on an individual's likelihood of sharing misinformation. Additionally, it assesses the influence of the official response to these fake news stories. The dataset comprises 333,944 messages gathered from Weibo regarding China's COVID-19 outbreak, processed through a comprehensive rumor identification algorithm. The findings indicate that sharing behavior is significantly shaped by personal attributes and the efficacy of official interventions. Specifically, the research highlights the impact of an individual's background, social connectivity, and reputation on sharing decisions, while also demonstrating that strong official actions can mitigate the viral spread of rumors. Ultimately, the study offers valuable insights and practical recommendations for preventing future digital misinformation outbreaks.

Planetary nebulae (PNe) serve as reliable tracers of stellar evolution and provide reliable distance measurements for their host galaxies. This study presents the most extensive collection of PNe ever identified within the galaxies of the Fornax Cluster, resulting in a total of 3,011 objects. These were categorized into three groups based on surface brightness: high (110 PNe), intermediate (1,332 PNe), and low (1,778 PNe) brightness. Automated scripts facilitated the distance assessment for 2,310 of these high-intermediate PNe, with human verification applied to 1,800 cases. The analysis reveals a pronounced gap in the distance distribution at approximately 8.5 Mpc, a feature likely caused by selection biases in the distance measurement process. Furthermore, the derived distance distribution aligns closely with those obtained from [OIII] emission line studies, yet the mean distance calculated in this work is systematically lower. This discrepancy may stem from an underestimation of velocity dispersion when using an automated method for large samples or an inherent bias in the traditional, sample-intensive techniques. Additionally, an algorithm was developed to classify PNe by evolutionary stage, which was subsequently employed to generate theoretical H-R diagrams for various galaxy populations. LifeFlow introduces a high-efficiency stream processing model designed to handle regular streams—streams characterized by a fixed processing window size. This approach replaces traditional infinite streams, which often require excessive memory and computational resources. LifeFlow utilizes a two-phase algorithm that first partitions data within the current window and subsequently performs processing only on the partitioned data. Benchmarks indicate that for common processing tasks, this regular stream can achieve a 100-fold reduction in memory usage and a tenfold improvement in processing speed.

This study investigates the absence of timelike Bertrand curves within spacetime. By restricting attention to parameterizations where arc length varies, any curve adhering to a constant tuple of radius and curvature radii—encompassing spirals and helices—cannot exist in Minkowski space. While the paper proves that no curve with retorted constant Frenet structure satisfies these conditions, it leaves the scenario where such constants do not apply unproven. Consequently, the specific case of timelike curves within the broader context of helicoids remains open.

The primary objective of this study is to investigate the impact of substituting standard convex loss functions, such as Mean Squared Error (MSE), for neural network classification tasks that typically rely on Cross-Entropy (CE). Although the CE loss is not new, it remains the preferred choice for classification due to its compatibility with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimization, whereas the MSE loss often is. While the theoretical equivalence between cross-entropy and softmax has been established for years, it remains surprising that researchers and practitioners continue to favor the standard configuration. To examine this issue, we conducted an experiment using the MNIST dataset, comparing the performance of both losses under identical conditions. The results indicate that cross-entropy and softmax/MSE yield nearly identical outcomes, confirming their practical interchangeability in this context. However, when applied to the ImageNet dataset, the MSE loss resulted in a significant decline in performance compared to the CE approach. This discrepancy led us to hypothesize that the MSE loss may perform differently on datasets with higher complexity and dimensions. To test this, we analyzed multiple datasets from the EMNLI collection for natural language classification tasks. The experiments revealed that cross-entropy consistently outperformed MSE across all cases, with the gap widening as dataset complexity increased. Finally, we explored the potential causes behind these observations, considering the specific characteristics of the losses and providing insights into why SGD may respond differently to MSE on large-scale problems.

The crystallization of polymers, whether occurring during processing or within the finished material, significantly influences their mechanical behavior and morphological characteristics. A primary driver for the formation of these structures is strain-induced crystallization (SIC), which notably enhances the durability of materials against tearing. To examine the connection between microstructure generation and resulting mechanical properties, this study employs a continuum-based framework that integrates thermomechanical constitutive models with nucleation and growth theories. This specific approach is applied to analyze uniaxial tension tests on natural rubber, demonstrating its capability to replicate the rising stiffness associated with SIC and the emergence of lamellar crystallites visible via transmission electron microscopy. Although this model relies on a specific material example, it offers a robust general tool for assessing the interplay between material constitutiveness and microstructural development.

Although traditional non-coherent differential detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM) is robust against synchronization delays, its bit error rate (BER) performance degrades significantly as that delay increases. This study investigates the detection performance of differential $\rm m$-TPM without coherence, focusing specifically on the delay tolerance of the classic minimum distance-based algorithm. Through both numerical simulations and analytical derivations, it is demonstrated that this traditional algorithm benefits from extended integration times achieved via longer symbol durations according to Razi's transformation. Consequently, by strategically manipulating duration within Razi's framework, one can enhance the differential detection tolerance to significant delays.

The vacuum compressibility of thermal systems is found to be non-zero when the quantum potential arising from Heisenberg's uncertainty principle acts as a force causing spacetime variability. Previously excluded from calculation using the standard Grand Canonical Ensemble due to the difficulty of determining the quantum potential for interacting systems, this paper addresses that challenge. It derives an explicit expression for the quantum potential within the Grand Canonical framework by solving the relevant Schrödinger equation through the method of Lagrangian dualization. Using the newly developed formula, the vacuum spacetime compressibility is computed specifically for the ideal photon gas.

ATOMIC represents a comprehensive corpus designed to showcase machine-atlased, if-then inferred common knowledge, drawn from 1,000 human-written entries describing AT work-related scenarios. Our study introduces ATNOTE, an efficient algorithm for automatically summarizing similar passages via "if"-condition and "then"-consequence extraction. Utilizing ATNOTE, we performed inter annotator verification on 1,000 segmented snippets, resulting in a structured knowledge base of 100 entries. Each rule encapsulates generalizable logic—for instance, Rule #1 states: "If AT work is at the home, at the work it is not at the home, at the work it is not at the work." This paper formally defines our ATNOTE method, the ATOMIC dataset, and provides an in-depth analysis of the inferred common knowledge.

Asset allocation stands as a classic application in finance and serves as an ideal test case for harnessing quantum computing capabilities in real-world scenarios. Recognizing that implementing the full Hahn–Liu algorithm (HHL) on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware is impractical due to hardware constraints, we instead introduce qHLL. This is a hybrid algorithm tailored specifically for Asset Allocation that runs efficiently on NISQ devices. Our study compares performance across three approaches: traditional methods using HHL, the hybrid variant qHLL, and standard heuristics. Results indicate that while these modern methods may not always beat heuristics in every situation, they significantly reduce both computational time and resource usage compared to the full HHL framework.

A sequence $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ of $n$-tuples of positive integers is designated as a parking function of length $n$ if the non-decreasing rearrangement $p'$ satisfies $p'_i \leq i$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$. This condition models $n$ drivers with preferred parking spots $p_k$ on a road containing exactly $n$ locations; driver $k$ attempts to park at $p_k + t$ for the smallest $t \geq 0$ such that the spot is unoccupied, ensuring everyone parks if and only if the sequence is valid. Although first observed by R.P. Stanley in 1989, the asymptotic behavior of the initial positions for uniform parking functions of length $n$ as $n \to \infty$ remained unstudied. This paper demonstrates that these initial positions converge in distribution to an exponential random variable with mean $1/2$, a result derived from the demonstration convergence to a specific piece-wise defined density function.

We report on the conductance of Niobium Nitride (NbN) superconducting nanowires, measured under both ambient and cryogenic vacuum conditions. Measurements taken at 4 Kelvin under various temperatures and gate voltages reveal conductance values of approximately $2e^2/h$ in air, which drops to approximately $1e^2/h$ when transferred to a chamber with controlled humidity and gases. Furthermore, conductance exhibits quantization as a function of gate voltage, while coherent quantum oscillations emerge in response to magnetic fields. Most notably, conductance switches between $2e^2/h$ and $0$ in discrete steps as the superconducting critical current is modulated. These conductance plateaus, combined with the observed charge sensitivity, provide conclusive evidence for the formation of a superconducting quantum interference device (SQUD) charge qubit.

Video forecasting involves predicting future visual content based on an input video clip, requiring an in-depth grasp of the clip's events, object interactions, and environmental context. This work introduces a novel hypothesis suggesting that certain aspects of the unseeable content can be anticipated by representing visible information through both a spatial layout and a temporal sequence. Specifically, our proposed approach, called Dual-Representative Forecasting (DRF), integrates representations in spatial layout and temporal sequence to forecast future content. We identify a top-down object detection model as the source for spatial layout data, while the temporal sequence is extracted via a bottom-up clipping technique. Although multiple potential source features exist, we found that objects and action—though invisible—are critical for anticipating unseen content. To measure the importance of these bottom-up and top-down outputs, we created an attention-based framework that evaluates how much each feature contributes to the task. Using this method, we discovered that temporal sequence data is more critical than spatial layout data for video forecasting. Consequently, we created a new dataset called Tuxedo, designed to evaluate how different feature types impact video forecasting outcomes. Finally, we proposed a novel architecture called Dual-Representative Video Forecasting (DRVF), which creates a weighted combination of spatial layout and temporal sequence representations to achieve superior performance on the challenging Next-10 challenge benchmark.

Inter-orbital interactions, where the energy levels of distinct orbitals influence one another, are a fundamental concept in condensed matter physics that has historically been explored using theoretical models. This study offers an experimental verification drawn from a dataset comprising 200,000 measurements of hydrogen's $p$ and $d$ spectral levels. An analysis of this extensive dataset reveals a pronounced and systematic interaction between the $p$ and $d$ orbitals of hydrogen. Furthermore, similar datasets generated through high-precision theoretical calculations exhibit comparable characteristics. Such datasets display pronounced visual patterns when viewed as two-level systems via Level Level Correlation (LLC) plots, which appear distinct from those observed in systems lacking mutual influence. Given the potential utility of LLC plots in identifying interactions within complex many-body quantum regimes, this work proposes viewing orbital level interactions through the framework of Level Level Correlation analysis.

The $\Omega^{-}$, composed of three strange quarks ($sss$), remains one of the most elusive and elusive particles in particle physics. Its elusive nature stems from its inability to participate in both weak and strong interactions, rendering it impossible to produce via processes involving light quarks. Despite the scarcity of experimental data, the $\Omega^{-}$ has garnered significant theoretical attention, with various models predicting its properties, including its electromagnetic characteristics. This work presents the inaugural application of stochastic variational approach and semi-relativistic quark model to investigate the spectral properties and magnetic moments of the $\Omega^{-}$. Our analysis yields predictions for its total energy spectrum, including $\Omega^{-}(2790)$ and $\Omega^{-}(2380)$, along with their respective partial wave decay modes and magnetic moments. These values offer improved alignment with available experimental findings. Moreover, our forecasted lifetime aligns closely with recent measurements from the Belle II experiment.

Accurate predictions of disease transmission on urban trains require realistic simulations of pathogen aerosol behavior, which is critical during health crises. While existing studies often rely on simplified models, we have implemented and validated a comprehensive computational framework that accounts for complex airflow patterns. By integrating experimental data and the detailed geometry of London's Tube system, this approach transforms Direct Standardized Volume (DSV)—a direct infection metric—into more actionable estimates. Specifically, we generated DSV-based infection probabilities for a standard influenza strain on the Overground line. The results indicate that actual likelihoods of infection can reach up to three times the values predicted by well-mixed approximations, highlighting the significant discrepancy introduced by ignoring airflow dynamics and offering a precise tool for future pandemic preparedness.

The scattering mechanisms occurring at interfaces and within bulk regions are demonstrated to significantly regulate spin-orbit interaction in engineered heterostructures. Specifically, modifying electron scattering at the boundary of the ferromagnetic metal/superconductor Niobium/Nickel system alters the magnitude of the proximal spin-orbit magnetic field generated by induced supercurrents. Consequently, variations in the bulk and interfacial scattering properties directly influence the Niobium/Nickel ferromagnetic switching behavior. This work highlights the critical role of interface and defect-based scattering dynamics in shaping spin-electric coupling phenomena.

Following the semi-classical W.K.B approximation, the study derives the corresponding radial equation. By implementing the d'Alambert (or d'Alambert) technique, the paper identifies the corresponding eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. Most significantly, it demonstrates that within the asymptotic large quantum number limit ($n\rightarrow \infty$), the system mimics the behavior of a particle in $d$-dimensional space under the generalized Coulomb potential. Conversely, in the limit of small quantum numbers ($n\rightarrow 0$), the behavior parallels that of the space under the Morse potential. The current study's findings are supported by corresponding graphical representations.

This study introduces a method to impose explicit Lipschitz constraints on neural networks by applying an additional loss term during training, designed to regulate the maximal change in output relative to input variations. This approach aligns with prior research highlighting that bounded Lipschitz constants enhance generalization and stability against adversarial examples. We demonstrate that such constraints can be effectively integrated into the backpropagation process. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical framework showing that minimizing a standard empirical risk with a weighted Lipschitz term is mathematically equivalent to regularizing it via a surrogate risk. Our findings indicate that an optimal weight parameterizes this surrogate risk, connecting it to established techniques like spectral normalization. Finally, our experiments reveal that enforcing Lipschitz consistency serves as a potent regularization strategy, particularly when training data is limited.
