Radiation exposure concerns and the higher costs associated with Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) frequently discourage individuals from undergoing both PET and MRI scans. Although recent studies often assume PET and MRI data are always available, this is rarely the case in clinical practice. Current approaches that merge limited- and reduced-dose PET data with structural MRI using neural networks fail when such multimodal datasets are missing, and existing methods relying solely on internal model corrections struggle with this limitation. To address these issues, we introduce a framework using reduced-dose PET scans paired with external MRI data, where the two modalities are aligned through uncertainty-aware, physics-inhibiting regression. This approach integrates a density estimation step to capture internal prior knowledge, along with transformation networks designed to integrate MRI features into the analysis. Our method offers several key benefits: it does not require MRI data for tasks where it is unavailable, utilizes external features to enhance performance through uncertainty-conscious multimodal training, utilizes out performance by incorporating explicit point-to-point intensity priors to ensure accuracy, and utilizes superior results through competitive metrics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this proposed method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques across multiple dimensions, including reduced-dose consistency, scaling capabilities, and general robustness.

Centering theory (Grosz et al., 1995) offers a robust framework for analyzing the local cohesion of conversation through the lens of coreference, yet its applicability to automatic coreference resolution remains under-investigated. This paper presents a novel neural coreference resolution model that integrates the operational mechanics of Centering Theory. Empirical results demonstrate that incorporating these features substantially improves performance on the MR dataset compared to a baseline. To address questions regarding the model's interpretability, we developed a method for visualizing coreference outcomes aligned with the centering structure of specific texts. These visualizations reveal that the integrated Centering Theory components effectively capture coreferencing patterns in the test data, confirming the system's capacity to represent such dynamics accurately.

WiFi signal strength fluctuates based on environmental factors, necessitating careful access point placement to ensure adequate coverage. This study introduces a novel approach utilizing Wireless Fidelity (WiFi) Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) data to evaluate the accessibility of various physical locations within an area. The proposed method employs machine learning to synthesize assessments of physical reachability using only RSSI inputs, eliminating the requirement for camera-based or sensor-based installations. Consequently, this cost-effective and efficient framework offers a practical solution for identifying navigable zones, with potential applications in search and rescue missions as well as facility management.

Beam fragmentation configuration effects on energy recovery linacs (ERLs) have long been recognized as a fundamental physical phenomenon. Nevertheless, their practical application in optimizing the configuration of energy recovery sections has remained limited. This work investigates the connection between fragmentation efficiency and specific machine parameters, including aperture dimensions, bunch charge, and transverse filling patterns. Research into varying aperture sizes demonstrates that smaller apertures enhance electron-positron interaction efficiency, thereby increasing emittance degradation. Similarly, changes in bunch charge reveal a non-linear relationship between charge density and efficiency, peaking at moderate levels before declining due to reduced density at high charges. Furthermore, different transverse filling patterns exhibit distinct efficiency profiles, with a single delta function pattern achieving the highest efficiency. Combining these findings, efficiency optimization allows for transverse emittance reduction by a factor of 10 through adjustments in aperture, bunch charge, and filling pattern. Consequently, such adjustments can significantly improve the performance of energy recovery linear accelerators.

We present the one-loop central-emission vertex for two gluons attached to an arbitrary external line in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, utilizing a recursive method based on master triangle and box coefficients previously introduced for the central-emission vertex involving one gluon and one fermion. Through integration-by-parts reductions, we demonstrate that the one-loop two-gluon vertex consists solely of scalar master integrals, confirming its real-valued nature across all kinematic regions. Furthermore, we establish a direct relation between the finite ${\rm{d}}\log$ form of this vertex and the discontinuities found in four dimensions, ultimately providing a compact expression for the vertex valid in any space-time dimension.

Strongly elongated polymers adsorbed onto solid surfaces create what are known as "polymer bristles." When these bristles are sufficiently long, a distinct boundary forms where the probability of finding a molten (unadsorbed) state drops to zero; this is the end-exclusion region. Using the method of dual variables, we have precisely determined the geometry of this region for an infinitely long, finite-width plate measuring $L \times W$, where the elongation $z$ far exceeds $W$. Although this calculation applies to that specific case, it serves as an accurate approximation for any surface elongation $z$ much greater than its characteristic dimension $R$. For objects of other shapes, we provide numerical results for elongations $z$ up to $1000$ times greater than $R$, allowing simulations to extend over significantly longer periods than previously feasible.

The metric dimension of a graph represents the smallest possible cardinality for a resolving set, with a resolving set defined as a vertex subset where every other vertex possesses a unique distance profile relative to the set's members. First posed in 1975 by Harary and Melter initially as an inquiry about the optimal coordinate system efficiency in a physical map, this concept has since garnered extensive research. For graphs exhibiting infinite cardinality, it is frequently the case that the minimum resolving set shares the same size as the graph's overall order. This article investigates the shortened metric dimension, defined through the requirement that the distance profile of any graph element compared to a resolving set must include only those distances non-zero for some element within the resolver. Our primary achievements involve determining the shortest resolving set sizes for complete bipartite graphs, paths extended with cycles attached to one side, and complete bipartite structures. Additionally, we establish several bounds applicable to graphs of unlimited extent.

Dictatorship mechanisms allocate resources by allowing agents to select items sequentially according to a fixed order, utilizing their revealed preferences to determine that position. While theoretically, full information about this ordering could yield Pareto improvements over serial dictatorship (SD), gathering such data is often impractical. Although previous research has explored more flexible data collection methods, it has been constrained to specific scenarios, such as single-agent multi-item contexts or particular preference structures. In this work, we propose and analyze a generalized setting where several agents compete for several items. We demonstrate the impossibility of achieving full information SD-efficiency when at least two agents and at least three items are involved. Conversely, for two items, we prove that truthfulness can be achieved in polynomial time. In cases with $m$ items, our trueful algorithms produce utility profiles exponentially closer to the exponent of $m$ compared to standard serial dictatorship. To validate practical effectiveness, we also present extensive numerical simulations.

Utilizing a sequence of 3.6-year *PS1* (Pan-STARRS1) archival images, this study investigates binary asteroid systems, with a specific emphasis on those containing companion objects too faint for direct visual confirmation in *PS1* data. The dataset encompasses 1,000 target asteroids, selected from *PS1* archives and re-examined via original, unprocessed master images. A manual inspection protocol identified 1,000 binary systems, yielding a fraction estimate of $f_{binary} = 0.33 \pm 0.0033$. Notably, 1,000 systems were identified where secondary components were too dim for direct detection during initial surveys. The resulting secondary-to-primary brightness ratio distribution peaks at $\Delta m = 0.99 \pm 0.0099$, suggesting a prevalence of mass-proportional binaries among this population. This finding offers a complementary dataset to existing studies, which typically focus on systems with easily resolvable secondaries.

This work defines and establishes the validity of a U-shaped neural network-based estimator designed for U-shaped network regression. This method integrates standard algorithms with a simple parameter to create a flexible framework capable of inferring U-shaped relationships among node attributes while maintaining U-shaped network regression. The paper begins with the recent advancement in regression using network regression data and introduces the proposed estimator, highlighting its connection to current methods and the benefits of adding the parameter. Subsequently, it outlines the conditions for the parameter and demonstrates that the U-shaped network regression data is asymptotically valid. Finally, it presents a finite sample analysis and simulation studies to illustrate the current method's effectiveness in network regression data.

Proteins are semi-flexible macromolecules whose functions depend on specific three-dimensional structures, which evolve through complex folding processes from linear chains. Since a single amino acid sequence can theoretically fold into multiple conformations, a fundamental inquiry involves how nature selects the one biologically active state. This study applies topology theory to investigate such "folding choices" within a model of knotted proteins featuring an inverse-repeating motif (IRM). An IRM is created by folding a protein loop back upon itself, allowing interactions between the original and reversed segments. We demonstrate that an IRM containing a hairpin configuration offers a topologically stable pathway connecting open and knotted states. Consequently, these hairpins act as "selection guides," ensuring that knoting occurs along a trajectory between the open and final forms that preserves the directionality of the repeating units. To validate this finding, we analyzed real-world examples of knotted proteins with IRMs, confirming that hairpin-induced guidance between open and closed states is biologically prevalent. We further propose a structural metric to quantify the topological affinity between pairs of segments within the context of knotting. Biologically, the suggested emphasis on hairpin-mediated orientation preservation between native open and closed forms suggests a functional mechanism for regulating the transition between these protein states.

For a symplectic manifold $(X, \omega)$, the symplectic mapping category group $\mathcal{C}(x,\sigma)$ is defined analogously to the Turaev cobranching number, measuring the complexity of removing spherical embeddings with a normal symplectic sphere. In this paper, we examine the distribution of these values for the spherical-free embedded symplectic blowups of $\mathbb{T}^2$, showing that their values are either 0, 1, 2, or 1/2. We provide explicit constructions for each outcome. We further demonstrate that $\mathcal{C}(x,\sigma)$ is bounded below by a newly identified, computationally simpler invariant, the 2-mapping category, calculating this value explicitly for 1/2, 0, and 1/2, and conjecturing it holds for all cases. We also explore the relationship between the mapping category category and the Turaev cobranching number.

Nambu-Goldstone theorems establish a fundamental divide between theories exhibiting them and those that do not, notably often separating geometric from non-geometric approaches. The theorem itself asserts that theories containing it necessarily host massless particles known as Nambu-Goldstone bosons, yet it fails to provide information regarding the specific Lagrangians required for these particles to exist without acquiring mass. To address this gap, I introduce a supplementary principle called the Irregular Nambu-Goldstone theorem. This principle applies universally to both relativistic and non-relativistic frameworks by distinguishing theories based whether they adhere to specific symmetry transformations—specifically, whether they observe "irregular" representations—rather than through mathematical formalism. The irregular representation implies a scenario where a continuous symmetry acts irregularly on a specific operator, typically one linked to an excited or irregular state. The additional principle asserts that the presence of an irregular symmetry representation guarantees the theory contains an infinite set of massless particles. I demonstrate the applicability of this principle by applying it to various cases, including QCD, where it clarifies the mechanism behind the disappearance and reappearance of certain particles as one moves between regimes.

We introduce a new method for generating text-based counterfactual examples using a 36-billion-word large language model (LLM) named GPT-3. Our approach, named DISCO, combines an iterative process with an innovative approach to evaluating counterfactual quality. Our results demonstrate GPT-3's ability to generate high-quality counterfactual examples across six distinct categories, including crime, health, education, employment, housing, and banking. We assessed the utility of these examples by measuring improvements in the decision-making capabilities of humans and machine classifiers. Specifically, we found that pre-training binary classifiers with our produced examples resulted in a 10% increase in their cross-domain robustness.

In reinforcement learning applied to open-domain dialogue systems, a common challenge is acquiring a comprehensive set of comprehensive rewards that accurately reflect user preferences. Traditionally, a single conversation turn is assigned one reward value, which implicitly assumes that a solitary reward is sufficient to guide the generation of an entire multi-turn conversation. However, this assumption risks an agent's inability to learn from its designated feedback label. Our research reveals that a single positive dialogue turn inherently contains multiple reward-associated attributes, a property we designate as "multi-label" data. To address this, we introduce a model designed to extract individual-label-based rewards for each specific attribute. By integrating these turn-specific attribute rewards into a reinforcement backbones, we aim to enhance the agent's alignment with human expectations. Empirical testing confirms that models trained using our approach outperform those using conventional reward structures in generating content that matches the themes of feedback labels.

This work presents a 2-categorical adjunction establishing an equivalence between two distinct frameworks for classical mechanics. The first approach defines the theory through physical quantities, treating configurations as algebraic structures derived from these observables. The second, more conventional approach constructs mechanics by identifying configurations first and defining observables as functions mapping over them.

This adjunction functions as an upgrade to Stone duality, specialized for commutative unital algebras over $\mathbb{R}$. It offers an alternative perspective to, and potential refinements of, approaches pioneered by Arnold, Kostant, and Coste-Journe. By framing mechanics within this higher-categorical language, one can explicitly characterize conserved quantities and symmetry transformations, while providing a rigorous demonstration that both formulations yield physically indistinguishable dynamics.

The primary source of high-energy gamma-rays in the nearby universe remains unknown, with only two exceptions: binary black hole systems containing compact stellar remnants and jets associated with supermassive black holes. This study investigates whether magnetically accreted disks feeding nearby galactic black holes can similarly generate high-energy radiation. We find that such disks produce gamma-rays when magnetic fields extract disk material along relativistic jets, creating shocks that emit gamma-rays via inverse Compton scattering off synchrotron self-radiation. Unlike traditional jet theories, this model predicts disk emission peaking in gamma-rays, whereas X-ray emission from the disk boundary remains weaker. Observations of galaxies NGC 315, IC 5056, and W 79 support this scenario, indicating that disks around these black holes emit more intensely in gamma-rays than in X-rays. Conversely, W 79 and IC 5056 show comparable disk emission levels across both bands. While we cannot yet confirm W 79 and IC 5056 host magnetically accreted disks, this hypothesis offers a viable explanation for the data regarding them and for gamma-ray excesses observed at GALEX and Fermi towards NGC 315.

Heart sounds are typically classified to evaluate cardiac well-being and detect abnormalities like murmurs. Conventional approaches rely on manual feature extraction and machine learning, yet they often yield limited performance. In contrast, deep learning techniques have proven more effective for audio classification tasks. Nevertheless, existing models face hurdles when processing raw heart sounds, electrocardiograms, or manually derived features. This study introduces a novel classification framework for heart sounds that utilizes Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) trained directly on raw phonocardiogram data after conversion to spectrograms. To enhance the discrimination of murmurs, the proposed method incorporates category-specific training with morphological deformation convolution to better capture abnormal patterns. Furthermore, the framework addresses interference noise inherent in recordings by integrating Single-Channel Sound Separation (SSS) to filter artifacts and segregate heart components. Evaluation across three standard datasets demonstrates the superiority of this approach over current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.8111.

Wearable health devices are increasingly integral to daily life, generating vast amounts of data that hold significant potential for improving individual well-being. However, effective health analysis is hindered by challenges such as data silos, privacy concerns, and the high costs associated with traditional collection methods. Although Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising solution to these issues, its current performance often falls short when applied to health tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce "FedHealth," a federated transfer knowledge framework designed to enhance cross-dataset generalization. FedHealth integrates federated transfer knowledge into the training process, utilizing it to bridge the distributional gaps between private, real-world wearable data and large-scale public datasets. Extensive experiments conducted across three distinct real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches in practical scenarios.

This study examines various portfolio improvement approaches designed to mitigate the issue of moment calculation exceedance in traditional models. We analyze the differences and commonalities among these methods, finding that most can be interpreted as implementations of the moments carrying over concept. Additionally, we investigate how the specific allocation of the residual moment affects overall portfolio performance.

This paper introduces the mathematical framework for a toggling irreversible stochastic switching problem involving càdlàg execution patterns. We formulate and analyze the core elements—including the value function, optimal switching strategies, and double value functions (specifically for both credible and hypothetical transactions)—to establish that all components satisfy a system of quasi-variational inequalities of tropical type. Furthermore, we formulate a novel certification theorem for optimal irreversible transactions that accommodates jumps in stock price movements.

The production mechanism involving lepton-flavor violation (LFV) is of significant interest within Beyond Standard Model (BSM) frameworks, with leptoquarks representing a prominent class of LFV operators. Such processes are forbidden by the standard SM; consequently, any observed LFV event at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) would definitively indicate the presence of new physics. We investigate uneven leptoquark pairs, where distinct lepton flavors appear in the pair-production process, highlighting how various LFV extensions of leptoquark models influence cross-section measurements. Our analysis demonstrates that leptoquark parameters defining LFV interactions significantly alter the magnitude of unequal production, potentially creating the appearance of an LFV absence in LHC data even when leptoquarks are present. To ensure optimal sensitivity for detecting these uneven-pair events, we have established refined LHC cut-and-weight strategies.

Using a population synthesis approach applied to the Extragalatic Molecular Gas Survey (EXGMGS), we examine the subthermal excitation of high-J CO lines within the molecular gas reservoirs of ExGMGS targets. We identify that in approximately 70\% of galaxies, the critical densities for transitions ($J\geq4$) exceed the local cosmic ray–generated UV field temperature ($T_{\rm cr}$). Consequently, these transitions are subthermally stimulated, implying that their emissivity is decoupled from the molecular gas mass density and is instead primarily dictated by the radiation field. We suggest leveraging the spatially resolved spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of these transitions to create a new, map-based metric for the "molecular cosmic ray–UV field strength." This proposed map offers a distinct advantage over existing methods: it targets the molecular gas phase specifically and relies on an emissivity mechanism that is insensitive to density variations. We hope this new tracer will significantly enhance current methodologies for assessing star formation potential.

This work investigates the series reconstruction challenge for permutations characterized by a Hamming-type measure of disorder. Within this framework, the disorder metric relies solely on the elements appearing in positions $1$ through $k$ of the target permutation $\sigma$. The objective is to ascertain whether there exists a reconstruction measure such that the expected disorder relative to the true permutation $\sigma$ minimizes itself uniformly across every possible distribution on the symmetric group $S_n$. Under certain technical constraints, the text outlines the construction of an algorithm achieving this uniform near-optimality with respect to the disorder metric.

Pulsar Timing Arrays are poised to enable the detection of gravitational waves originating from massive black hole mergers characterized by high orbital eccentricities. To analyze data for these signals, we have developed "GEO-RECCEN," a novel C++/Python package designed to calculate post-Newtonian-accurate celestial elements and true anomalies for highly eccentric systems. Although GEO-RECCEN proves approximately ten times more computationally intensive per data point than standard linear interpolation or quadratic splining splines, it remains roughly one hundred times faster per point compared to our own previous signal interpolator. In a quadratic spline comparison, signal recovery was found to be 99.99% effective; specifically, a 1% amplitude drop occurred only during extremely limited, pessimistic scenarios involving very short observation spans (0.1 times the orbital period) and high total counts (1000s). Consequently, while linear methods suffice for circular orbits or data with low signal-to-noise ratios, analyzing highly eccentric mergers demands the precision provided by GEO-RECCEN to mitigate amplitude biases caused by interpolation errors.

The ASEP speed procedure involves defining jump rates as continuous functions of system size, thereby creating a framework applicable to nearly all multi-step asymmetric simple exclusion processes. This approach enables the use of local limit techniques to analyze a broad class of initial conditions, including those that are piecewise deterministic. Additionally, it is applicable to second-order processes, such as those defined by multiple classes of particles.

Mathematical epidemiological models offer a spectrum of structures, each with distinct advantages and constraints. This article introduces a classification system for these epidemics based on five core pillars: compartment definitions, transmission terms, initial conditions, system boundaries, and numerical techniques. Applying this framework to recent outbreaks reveals a trend toward replacing classic SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) systems with more intricate approaches. The article explores the benefits and drawbacks associated with various transmission functions, including those grounded in individual-based and agent-based methodologies. Finally, given the ongoing global SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, the author argues for the adoption of more sophisticated modeling paradigms rather than merely translating the simplified SIR framework into systems governed by individual dynamics.

The control of atom interactions through the adjustment of electronic band structures offers promising avenues for spinor and fermionic atoms, groups that are inherently limited by severe recombination rates. This work presents the conversion of sing spin atoms into molecules utilizing selectively tuned lasers. By establishing an interaction imbalance between the singlet and triplet spin states of two colliding atoms, a sing three-body recombination route is identified that facilitates deep suppression of atom-to-molecule conversion. Theory demonstrates feasibility via rubidium atoms as a model system, suggesting this spin-selective mechanism operates universally across various atomic species.

Although DNA storage represents a promising new paradigm for data archival, developing effective and efficient software tools for encoding remains a significant hurdle. This study introduces HiEncode, an innovative coding framework specifically designed to streamline and accelerate DNA data storage by leveraging hierarchical encoding. Traditional methods typically rely on monolithic, large-scale lookup tables containing thousands of gigabytes of base pair mappings, which creates prohibitive memory constraints for current computing architectures. In contrast, HiEncode partitions these extensive tables into a structured tree, decomposing large tables at the root node into progressively smaller tables at child nodes until reaching small, character-level mappings at the leaves. This strategic organization significantly alleviates the memory burden, rendering high-capacity storage feasible with existing hardware. Furthermore, empirical results demonstrate that the coding process itself generates useful patterns, which HiEncode effectively exploits through a predictive model based on Markov Chains to forecast storage sequences. By integrating this structured approach with robust prediction capabilities, the system achieves a 20% reduction in encoding errors compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Resolving partial differential equations (PDEs) serves as a fundamental step in addressing various physical challenges. While traditional approaches like finite element methods, finite difference schemes, and finite volume methods are well-established, they often require extensive training and take considerable time to implement. In contrast, deep learning techniques enable rapid model training and can generalize to unseen data. This study introduces a deep learning-based solver designed to solve the shallow water equations (SWEs). The proposed model is trained on a dataset generated using a conventional finite difference method and successfully demonstrates the capacity to generalize to novel initial and boundary conditions. Furthermore, the paper presents a novel technique for reconstructuring solutions from the network's latent output, ensuring smoothness across the solution field. Our findings reveal that this SWE solver operates approximately 1000 times faster than a standard finite difference algorithm while preserving high accuracy. Additionally, it offers a visual interpretation of the trained model's internal structure through the analysis of latent space representations and the mapping functions.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging multiple exposures of a single scene, allowing bright regions exceeding the sensor's limits to remain visible while preserving detail in dark areas. This work introduces a system that automatically determines exposure selections and High-dynamic-range synthesis using a standard smartphone camera. First, the method estimates the scene's dynamic range by inferring the histogram of natural exposure. It then calculates the optimal number of exposures and the specific delta-shutter values required to create a range sufficient for HDR merging. Finally, the proposed algorithm for range estimation and parameter optimization is evaluated against current approaches, with comparative results demonstrating its effectiveness.

Neural networks have proven highly effective at solving complex tasks, yet their "black box" nature limits our ability to understand the underlying mechanisms. This understanding becomes even more elusive when traditional mathematical models are unavailable. To address this, we introduce a framework for developing models that are both capable and interpretable through purely data-driven methods. We term this approach Causal Neural Learning (CNL). CNL integrates structural elements drawn from domain-specific knowledge into a neural architecture, guiding training to align with specified causal principles. We demonstrate the utility of this method across three distinct scenarios: eliminating spurious correlations, adapting to distributional shifts, and handling missing data. Although CNL functions as a general framework applicable to various scenarios, we also provide concrete implementations using state-of-the-art models. These exemplars illustrate how to embed targeted causal structures into neural networks and highlight key design decisions for integrating such inducible structures. Finally, we offer a survey of common structural elements and discuss their use in creating more interpretable, cognitively aligned AI systems.

Reducing preconditioning errors is essential for accurately solving cardiac mechanical problems using cardiac finite element methods. This study offers a comparative analysis of two multilevel preconditioning techniques: a hierarchical approach and a hierarchical method with a diagonal preconditioner applied to the mass matrix. These strategies are evaluated against a cardiac mechanical model that simulates uniaxial, equibiaxial, and Arruda-Boyce hyperelasticity. Results indicate that both multilevel preconditioners substantially decrease the condition number compared to solving the linear system directly with a highly nonlinear elastic constitutive law. Furthermore, a diagonal-matrix implementation of the hierarchical method retains significantly higher solution accuracy than the standard hierarchical method while requiring roughly 95% less computational time. Consequently, the diagonal-matrix approach demonstrates clear advantages in efficiency and performance over the existing hierarchical method.

Standard Brownian motion, where a random walk's total displacement variance equals the sum of individual step variances, exhibits Normal diffusion. In contrast, Brownian motion adhering to a Gaussian random walk displays anomalous, or non-Normal, diffusion when total variance differs from the additive rule of step variances. This study investigates the characteristics of non-Normal Brownian motion in the context of fluid percolation through a porous medium. The analysis reveals that anomalies emerge specifically when the duration of Brownian motion varies randomly; an exact formula is provided linking the variance of total displacement to the permeability variations of the medium relative to its mean. Additionally, the study explores how varying statistical distributions of logarithmic durations and medium permeability impact anomalous diffusion exponents.

This approach determines mode characteristics by identifying the eigenvalues and eigenmodes of a specific operator constructed from the transverse parts of the paraxial Helmholtz equation. We illustrate this method by deriving the modes for various waveguide and resonator types, including a new formulation for rectangular waveguides based on hypergeometric functions. Additionally, we analyze the interplay between guided modes and resonant frequencies, an aspect crucial for designing integrated photonic devices. The outcomes presented here constitute an essential theoretical foundation for the work detailed in our accompanying publication.

Although the majority of reinforcement learning (RL) advancements rely on randomized testing for validation, these benchmarks suffer from rigidness, lacking both standardization and innovation. To tackle this issue, we introduce L2Explorer, a reference RL environment constructed upon real-world traffic data from an actual internet service provider's peering point. We demonstrate the modular design of L2Explorer, which enables the rapid integration of new synthetic traffic patterns and queue management disciplines. Additionally, we present an in-depth analysis exploring how RL algorithms react to various traffic engineering strategies. L2Explorer serves as a robust platform for assessing queue management solutions and validates itself as a potent supplement to existing reinforcement learning evaluations.

Declarative programming, which emphasizes describing the desired outcome rather than the execution path, has gained significant traction in recent years. This approach offers distinct advantages, such as enhanced modularity, code conciseness, and built-in parallelism. Nevertheless, these very attributes can complicate the debugging process. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel exploratory mechanism designed to assist developers in resolving errors within declarative applications. By leveraging event streams, the proposed technique dynamically visualizes the internal operational flow of these programs. The method dynamically generates a stream representing each variable within the code; it subsequently merges this multi-stream framework into a unified view by applying stream transformations that mirror the relationships between variables. The article outlines the technical design of this mechanism, demonstrates its practical implementation in Elm using the Forestry library, and offers a comparative analysis against existing dynamic debuggers.

We examine the family of $n$-parameter elliptic surfaces constructed from generalized Hill's equations. The text analyzes the relationship between their apparent varieties and the J-invariant, focusing specifically on the case where $n=3$. In this scenario, the apparent variety forms a torus, allowing the family to be expressed in Weierstrass normal form. By identifying the $j$-invariant along the various axes of the parameter space, we delineate the structures of isospectral classes. The paper concludes by comparing the resulting decompositions into these tori against the compactification achieved via algebraic methods.

Using a dataset of 10,000 early-type galaxies (ETGs) drawn from the CALIFA project, we examine the dependence of stellar mass formation on ($M_{*}-\text{SFR}$), focusing specifically on how bulge characteristics influence this relationship. Our findings indicate that ETGs exhibiting supergiant bulges possess significantly lower stellar masses for a given SFR compared to those dominated by disks or possessing minor bulges. Consequently, bulge fraction emerges as a primary determinant shaping the overall $M_{*}-\text{SFR}$ trend. Furthermore, when normalizing galaxy samples by their bulge fraction, the distinct "knee" or turnover seen in the M*-SFR curve for galaxies with prominent bulges becomes apparent at super solar masses ($\sim 10^{10.5} M_\odot$), a feature notably absent in populations of low bulge fractions. These observations imply that bulges drive the cessation of star formation in early-type systems at elevated mass thresholds. Regarding the physical mechanisms behind this decline, our results favor the theory that feedback from massive black holes—rather than the removal of gas due to stellar radiation pressure—is the dominant cause.

This study examines cross-language sentiment classification, specifically focusing on translating English text to Spanish to train and evaluate models. The authors address this as a multilabel classification task, allowing single sentences to be assigned multiple sentiment labels simultaneously. To this end, they developed two unique neural network architectures based on Convolutional Neural Networks designed specifically for translating sentences from English to Spanish text. The trained models demonstrate effectiveness in assessing sentiment across several datasets, including translated versions. Furthermore, the paper explores various training strategies, highlighting that multitask learning approaches using related text problems improve performance compared to single-task training. Overall, this research offers insights into how to effectively transfer knowledge between languages through shared training objectives.

X-ray radiographs are frequently utilized for diagnosing COVID-19; however, the ability to integrate these images with other clinical data for predicting outcomes has remained largely unexamined. This study investigates the feasibility of incorporating X-ray imagery alongside demographic and clinical information to forecast ICU admission in individuals infected with COVID-19. We compiled a dataset involving 1,142 patients, for whom we gathered X-rays, age, gender, symptoms, confirmed ICU status, and infection with or without influenza. Notably, 38.3% of the individuals required an ICU bed, with 16.8% admitted specifically due to COVID-19. We evaluated multiple machine learning models, integrating features derived from image analysis with clinical and demographic variables. Our results indicate that combining X-ray features with clinical data significantly enhances prediction accuracy compared to using clinical data alone, achieving an AUROC score of 0.81 (95% CI: 0.78–0.85) for distinguishing COVID-19 cases requiring ICU care from those not requiring it. Furthermore, using the same criteria to differentiate confirmed COVID-19 ICU admissions from non-ICU patients yielded an equivalent AUROC of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.76–0.83). These findings demonstrate that the identified X-ray image characteristics effectively identify severe COVID-19 requiring ICU intervention.

Visual association detection aims to identify whether a specific object exists in an image based on a recognized class of object. Although the potential applications are vast, current models often fail when confronted with "erroneous positives"—instances where the system incorrectly identifies a target object that is merely a fragment, unrelated piece, or synthetic element rather than a complete entity. These challenges primarily arise from training data containing flawed examples and the lack of mechanisms to distinguish between genuine objects and partial components. This paper introduces an analytical framework designed to dissect the root causes behind such erroneous positives and proposes novel strategies to mitigate them. Evaluations conducted across three diverse datasets demonstrate that the suggested approach substantially lowers the rates of false-positive detections compared to existing baseline models.

Utilizing multi-band imaging and integral field spectroscopy, the authors examined a galaxy within an galaxy cluster at redshift $z \sim 3$. The target system exhibits a classic two-component morphology consisting of an old, dense central region surrounded by a vast, quiescent stellar halo characterized by low stellar scatter and moderate unevenness ($\sigma_{\rm FPE} \sim 0.6\,\rm G\,y$). While the bulge component dates back to the epoch of enrichment ($t \sim 900\,\rm Myr$), the surrounding disk formed more recently ($t \sim 700\,\rm Myr$). The authors infer that an early disturbance triggered intense star formation in the central region, generating the bulge, whereas the outer disk settled afterward, accounting for its low velocity dispersion. This scenario mirrors findings from local galaxies regarding the formation bulges through significant creation events in disk systems. Furthermore, the system's unevenness and velocity dispersion align with predictions from the classic two-stage cluster formation model, suggesting that similar processes govern the development of structural components in similar systems at higher redshifts.

The ground-based detection of proton jets accompanying intense solar flares offers a method to decompose SDC (solar dose curves). This approach enables the separation of proton contributions from electron-photon energy and nuclear radiation, such as gamma rays and solar neutrons. This specific neutral component was difficult to detect from Earth during the November 11, 2004, X-class flare due to significant atmospheric absorption. However, the D3 Neutron Monitor Station in Tibet, China, successfully recorded a notable spike in neutron counts during the proton jet associated with an F10 flare on November 7, 2004. This study utilizes the timing profiles of protons and D3 neutron count data, alongside a model of atmospheric absorption, to construct a theoretical framework for these observations. The model determines the energy distribution of protons and neutral photons that yield matching projections in proton and neutron time histories. Validation against the event shows that the derived energy distribution of the proton jet aligns well with independent estimates from ground-based hard X-ray and gamma-ray spectra.

Toyz is an unusual, young A-type star known for its massive, wide-orbit super-Jovian companions. Its rapid rotation and the extreme spins of its planets suggest significant angular momentum within the planetary system. However, Toyz's unexpectedly slow rotation remains puzzling given the presence of these large planets and the short system age. We demonstrate that excess irradiation from the inner system planets likely causes atmospheric inflation and reduced opacity in the stellar atmosphere, mimicking spectral features of planetary absorption. Furthermore, the close proximity of these inner planets suggests tidal interactions may have spun the stars up to very high rates early in the system's history.

The proliferation of news sharing on social media platforms has significantly accelerated the dissemination of information, yet it has simultaneously given rise to a critical vulnerability: the production and spread of fake news. This phenomenon threatens the stability of societies and the effective functioning of democratic systems. Although existing research offers various strategies for identifying news veracity, the majority depends exclusively on textual content, thereby overlooking the supplementary information frequently embedded in shared multimedia. This limitation is particularly pertinent given that a substantial volume of news is distributed alongside images and videos. In this study, we introduce a framework for detecting news authenticity that effectively integrates and leverages cross-modal data—specifically, the synergistic use of both text and multimedia elements. Furthermore, we propose a novel meta neural process architecture tailored for emergent task generalization in scenarios involving new or unseen counterfeit content. This advanced approach is designed to quickly adapt to fresh detection challenges utilizing minimal samples, even when those samples lack corresponding multimedia. The recent discovery of silicon valley states offers a promising avenue for advancing quantum computing and novel electronic devices. To address the challenge of creating realistic brain abnormalities, we introduce Cerebral Adversarial Lesion Generation (CAGL), a method designed to simulate intracranial pathologies within the human brain structure. To this purpose, we integrate a Adverse Variational Auto-Encoder (Vae) with a segmentation encoder. The proposed model incorporates a feedback mechanism between the segmentation encoder and the generator, ensuring that lesion patterns align accurately with anatomical boundaries. Furthermore, we optimize the adversarial feedback loop by utilizing an image discriminator and a lesion presence detector. These components collectively guarantee that the synthesized pathology adheres strictly to neuroanatomical plausibility and exhibits convincing signs of disease. Extensive testing on the ADNI dataset confirms the model's superior performance compared to other approaches in terms of distribution fidelity, lesion realism, and clinical utility.

The G²F (or G²) system represents a novel, automated C/C++ compiler engineered specifically to accelerate Graphical Processing Units (GPU) performance. Although the source code for G²F remains confidential, its internal mechanisms are inferred to operate by first translating C++ input into an intermediate representation (IR). From this IR, the enhanced compiler automatically extracts and applies various GPU optimization strategies during the generation of final PTX code. This paper offers an in-depth analysis of the G²F Enhanced Compiler, detailing the identified optimizations and their implementation logic within the system.

Attribute extraction involves identifying and retrieving pertinent information from an attribute's potential value set, a skill that proves highly valuable in applications like intelligent question-answering and machine-assisted writing. Our proposed unified structure for attribute extraction relies on a contrastive learning framework designed to identify the most suitable values. Specifically, we treat the selection of a specific attribute value as a contrastive learning task, where pushing the text-attribution value pairs apart that are not suitable and keeping text-attribution value pairs close that fit improves textATtribution. To implement this approach, we established a specific structure for representing textATtribution candidate values and created an encoding architecture designed specifically for ATtribution candidate. In addition, we outline a unified framework for contrastive learning textATtribution. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across three distinct tasks: extracting party member affiliations, characterizing political leaders, and describing US presidents.

In the realm of high-dimensional modeling, categorical data is prevalent, yet existing approaches often fall short by either ignoring these features or treating every level of each category as an independent group. This study introduces a unified and flexible framework designed to tackle the challenges associated with categorical information. Our method employs a grouping structure that consolidates all levels of a specific category, ensuring that unrelated categories remain sparsely connected in terms of their effects, while different levels within the same category share coefficient estimates. We utilize the proposed approach across various regression models, demonstrating its practical application with Gaussian, Poisson, and generic loss functions. To handle the resulting non-convex optimization issues, we developed efficient algorithms that guarantee convergence to stationary points. Extensive experiments on both synthetic datasets and real-world case studies highlight the method's superior performance and illustrative capabilities compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. These findings confirm enhanced model accuracy alongside improved interpretability when analyzing categorical data.

Large language models (LLMs) possess impressive capabilities, yet their high computational costs and carbon footprint necessitate continuous improvement. A primary obstacle to progress is the difficulty in diagnosing failure causes and implementing effective remedies. This paper introduces Skill, a technique for embedding human-derived insights into larger models to facilitate their refinement. Skill integrates structured "skill tokens" into input data, allowing models to internalize specific external knowledge associated with these tokens. By training on datasets enriched with such skill tokens and linked knowledge, a model can leverage this information to resolve tasks it previously handled poorly. We tested Skill by injecting failure-correction insights into an 8-billion parameter variant of Llama 3, resulting in performance gains across various natural language generation tasks compared to baseline versions. We further demonstrate that models benefit significantly from targeted failure insights, particularly those affecting larger, more expansive variants.

Although vector maps are inherently free of aliasing for individual lines and polygons, artifacts emerge at line junctions where features meet or overlap. While existing research has addressed anti-aliasing for lines and fills separately, no solution effectively handles the connection between line features. This paper introduces a method to render connections between line segments by merging simple and joined commands, utilizing internal map topology data to construct a seamless, aliased-free bridge between segments.

Drawing upon recent research that has enhanced speech quality using deep neural networks and advanced acoustic modeling, this study focuses on dual-aspect refinements: spatial and temporal domains. To capture spatial features, we implemented a spectrum of convolutions within a deep neural network to identify speech patterns. For temporal characteristics, we incorporated Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). Our proposed Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN) integrates these components to jointly model both feature types, specifically targeting monophone speech embedded in noisy audio from a specific microphone channel. Evaluated on the high-fidelity demic AN4 database, results indicate superior performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, an ablation study confirms that integrating both convolutions and RNNs yields the most significant gains.

This study investigates a test case for atmospheric circulation modeling featuring a convective free surface and a stable free lower boundary, with both interfaces subjected to thermal non-equilibrium. We examine a scenario comprising air above water, where heat exchange across boundaries is dynamically determined. Our analysis highlights that this interface thermal non-equilibrium arises from a mismatch between the heat fluxes supplied by the air and water layers. We implement a model incorporating interfacial heat non-equilibrium, which accounts for thermal and shear discontinuities at the interface governed by boundary energy conservation. This approach includes an additional degree of freedom: the temperature of the air-water interface itself. In our dimensionless framework, we relate this interfacial temperature to the standard Rayleigh number and the Prandtl numbers of both fluids. The model is simulated using a single-column setup, revealing that the degree of thermal non-equilibrium is primarily dictated by the Prandtl number and fluid arrangement, whereas the Rayleigh number and viscosity contrasts have minimal impact. We identify two distinct convection regimes: at low values of interfacial thermal resistance, a regime with an isothermal interface and a single dominant roll exists; conversely, high interfacial thermal resistance triggers a regime characterized by interfacial hot spots, air-water thermal non-equilibrium, and secondary circulation rolls perpendicular to the primary ones. The study concludes by suggesting that this addition of interfacial temperature as a degree of freedom facilitates the extension to more complex multi-fluid atmospheric circulation models.

Generating photon-number entanglement between initially uncorrelated and separable multi-level atoms interacting via Jaynes-Cummings coupling is examined. We demonstrate that mutual entanglement arises when the sum of the atomic excitation levels exceeds the conserved total excitation of the coupled atom-light system. Analytical conditions are established for entanglement across various atom configurations, supported by a newly defined entropic uncertainty relation applicable to any number of levels. We further prove that full entangment of both atoms and the light field occurs when the collective atomic excitations are sufficiently high relative to one another. Finally, we show that complete entangment of the atoms can be achieved even if the light field remains partially distinguishable.

360-degree video streaming offers immersive advantages, yet it consumes excessive bandwidth. To mitigate this, selective downloading of unviewed areas based on user gaze patterns is essential. While prior research has largely concentrated on games and single-user scenarios, there is a notable absence of study regarding virtual travel videos involving multiple users and subtitles. This work investigates such videos by proposing a subtitles-based viewport prediction framework designed to enhance efficiency in multi-user contexts. We constructed a novel dataset featuring not only a guided tour of a historical temple with subtitles and participants, but also corresponding eye-tracking data. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between reader progress through subtitles and the actual viewed regions, demonstrating that subtitle interaction effectively predicts user viewing areas. Consequently, we suggest integrating subtitle information into bandwidth-optimization strategies for 360-degree virtual travel experiences.

Decision-based white-box attacks represent a significant advancement in black-box transfer scenarios, enabling more effective knowledge gain from other systems. However, this approach currently relies on gradient approximations that demand access to the target model's internal implementation, a constraint that is unattainable in genuine distributed environments. Furthermore, we establish that DC-Adam efficacy in acquiring external knowledge improves as architectural congruence between source and target systems increases.

Object-oriented robots are experiencing a surge in the development of observational learning techniques, primarily driven by the widespread adoption of large-scale remote assistance platforms. However, these current methods are ill-equipped to train autonomous agents for tasks involving real physical objects, as they fail to capture the dexterity, speed, and diversity inherent in human operators. Conversely, within the field of object-oriented skill generation through reinforcement learning, recent strategies for creating synthetic human demonstrations have not been adapted for real-world hardware. To address these gaps, we introduce a framework for capturing object-based demonstrations via a collaborative system. This system enables two operators to simultaneously control a robot and the task environment, thereby recording demonstrations that a single skilled operator would traditionally provide. We validate the superiority of these co-observed demonstrations by applying them to train a model using Reinforcement Learning for complex manipulation challenges. The resulting policy significantly outperforms those derived from demonstrations extracted from existing online assistance platforms.

This paper introduces a new metric, called the Probabilistic And Correct (PAC) code, which serves as a functional equivalent to the widely recognized Proportional Allocation with Cut-off (PAC) code used in fair division. Unlike the non-deterministic nature of the original computation, the proposed metric allows for consistent, deterministic calculation. The paper establishes theoretical bounds for this metric and presents an efficient algorithm to derive the deterministic PAC values. Furthermore, it explores the metric's implications within political science, offering relevant determinations based on its stable properties.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) tends to generate generic, uninformative expansions during translation; we suggest applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) with large-scale action spaces to resolve this issue. We introduce a rule-based filtering mechanism to eliminate invalid expansions and structure an RL framework with an extensive action design for training high-quality translations. Experimental results on the WMT 2019 Neural Machine Translation English-Chinese shared task demonstrate that our approach secures the top rank among all participants. Additionally, analyses of generated text quality and translation specifics confirm that RL with extensive actions substantially enhances translation fluency and quality.

A finding by Kierstead and Tannenberg demonstrates that when $p$ is sufficiently large relative to $q$, any two sets of size $p$ can be distinguished using a specific identifying test chosen from a collection $\mathcal{C}$ of size $2^{O(p)}$. MongoDB is a leading NoSQL database known for its document-oriented model, high scalability, and flexible schema. Nevertheless, it lacks full transactional support by default, which can compromise data consistency. This study introduces the validation of transactional assurance in MongoDB by analyzing a production environment handling billions of operations. The research examines the relationship between oplog windows and bulk write operations to confirm whether transactions execute with serializability. Findings indicate that while standard unacknowledged bulk writes within an oplog window may violate serializability, all other tested transaction types maintain serializational integrity.

This study investigates a model of triangular-based short-range repulsive interactions occurring between particles in two dimensions. This system exhibits a concealed geometric arrangement that drives a transition from a crystalline lattice to an amorphous state, contrasting with typical two-dimensional models where such interactions usually favor crystallization. Unlike the component particles, which possess an individual concave shape, the composite units, formed by their mutual interactions, display a convex structure. Dynamically, this model promotes the self-assembly into highly dense, stable structures characterized by triangular motifs. Uniquely, this model serves as a prototype for understanding self-reversal processes in both the orientational order and positional arrangement of particles. Distinct from previous models, this one does not necessitate an attractive potential to induce self-crystallization into dense triangular lattices; instead, self-reversal here results in the formation of an amorphous solid. We propose a new classification scheme for two-dimensional self-reversal models, identifying this as a "mutual and triangular case." The model's capacity to drive self-reversal without attractive forces suggests its utility in creating nanoassemblies containing metallic, magnetic, or chiral components, thereby enabling the construction of dense, ordered clusters featuring such elements.

Understanding how energy moves through solar atmospheric layers is crucial for explaining the unusual heating patterns of the solar atmosphere and corona. Although recent advancements from ground-based observatories, the Stereoscope, and the Solar Terrestrial Missions (including SOHO, Ulysses, and WIND) have significantly improved our grasp of energy distribution across the solar atmosphere, the inner heliosphere remains poorly understood due to lack of in-situ data. The PARS (Parker Solar Probe), currently the only mission capable of penetrating the inner corona, provides unique insights into these processes. Initial PARS data supports this hypothesis, revealing significantly higher turbulence intensities in radial breeze components compared to their azimuthal counterparts during the initial two encounters.

Speech-emotion recognition (RER) encounters significant challenges when transferring from large, diverse domains to specific target applications. We propose a hybrid approach combining Domain Adversarial Neural Network (DAN) and Deep Reinforcement Learning (FRL) to bridge this domain gap. First, the DAN method adapts the reward agent in the FRL system by reducing reliance on task-specific training data. Subsequently, the calibrated agent leverages Reinforcement Learning to refine RER performance. Evaluated across four distinct datasets, results demonstrate that this RFR+DAN method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms.

These equations of motion are further used to determine the initial configurations required to generate a stable shock upon void expansion. Our findings indicate that a stable shock can emerge regardless of whether the fluid follows a polytropic equation of state or exhibits varying heat flux and conductivity. Finally, we compare the resulting hydrodynamic expansion with that of acoustic wave propagation in an unvoided medium.

Interstellar panspermism involves the transfer of life between stars via a resilient, self-replicating seed, which could significantly impact planetary biosphere formation. The event shape engineering (ESE) technique allows researchers to examine the dynamics of particle production in heavy ion collisions by selecting collision systems with specific characteristic values. This paper investigates binary power control within $K$-user interference networks, aiming to identify how it alters the ultimate Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) compared to continuous power regulation. We introduce an applicable outer bound and validate it through GDoF equivalents and precise asymptotic analysis for large $K $. Our results demonstrate that optimal binary control yields a GDoF gap of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ over continuous control, with the advantage growing increasingly significant as the network expands. Specifically, the benefit per node peaks when traffic loads are unbalanced, favoring scenarios where some users are heavily congested while others are lightly loaded.

This study introduces a time-step adaptation approach for particle collision handling in particle-resolved direct numerical simulations (PR-DNS), ensuring physically accurate contact durations while maintaining computational efficiency through variable integration intervals. During collision events, the particle time step is automatically adjusted to satisfy a specific criterion for contact duration, remaining constant throughout the particle trajectory. The proposed method was first validated against an analytical elastic collision model and subsequently applied to assess its impact within gas-solid flow scenarios. Results confirm that adhering to the contact duration criterion aligns particle drag forces with those obtained using uniformly reduced time steps. Furthermore, the adaptive method yields nearly identical volume-averaged flow structures and particle concentration distributions compared to uniform stepping, yet achieves these physical accuracies with a roughly 30% reduction in total computation time.

This paper establishes the existence of integer sequences $\{x_n\}$ and $\{y_n\}$ that satisfy $x_n^2 + x_ny_n + y_n^2 = 7^n$. To demonstrate a fundamental whole-number property of this identity, it further proves that $x_n + (x_n+1)i$ yields an exact $7$-th power within the integer ring $\mathbb{Z}[i]$. This study introduces a control strategy designed to maximize the force a one-stick jumper can apply while bouncing off yielding ground. By modeling the ground as an elasto-plastic material, we first simulate the interaction between the stick's tip and the surface to calculate the maximum possible reaction force. Concurrently, we simulate the stick's flexible structure to analyze its tip behavior. These findings establish the strict force and tip constraints that a foot of the stick must respect during jumping. The control approach itself integrates a model-predictive controller with a tip-force strategy, which utilizes a stick yield model to identify the peak elastic storage energy. This mechanism ensures that just before full plastic deformation occurs, the foot reaches its highest velocity to take full advantage of the stored energy. We validate the proposed method through simulations and comparative analyses against other strategies, demonstrating significant improvements in jump height. Finally, we present preliminary experimental data from a built physical prototype to corroborate the simulation results.

Our approach integrates the Nambu-Jona-Lancosh string model with the stochastic color flux tube model to describe vector states, while treating condensed quark-antiquark condensates as a perturbation applied to these configurations. This method yields predictions for various charm-meson processes that align well with outcomes derived from perturbative QCD. Furthermore, we derive shape factor results for heavy-to-light transitions involving $b$ quarks that are consistent with findings from the stochastic color flux tube approach.

Researchers have proposed several approaches to determine hierarchy levels within information by utilizing text expandability—the phenomenon where certain words prompt the retrieval of related content. This paper introduces a new model based on the semantic field expansion method, designed to more accurately reflect temporal and conceptual growth in data. Empirical testing on a large-scale web crawl indicates that the new model substantially outperforms existing strategies, achieving a 0.033 improvement in F1 score compared to the best current method.

Quench dynamics track how a system evolves from an initial state toward its final equilibrium, a method valuable for identifying initial configurations with rapid equilibration. In this study, we apply quench dynamics to the precise cover problem annealed under both local and global perturbations applied to the final Hamiltonian. By analyzing the connection between dynamics and energy flow, we map out the "quantum annealing interval"—the temperature range where annealing outperforms thermalization. Our findings indicate that quench dynamics yield comparable results to standard annealing across most of this interval; however, at lower temperatures within the range, both annealing and quench dynamics demonstrate a clear advantage over waiting for thermal equilibrium.

The superconducting properties of the nickelate $\text{La}_3\text{NiO}_6$ are investigated within a dual-band model, focusing on the influence of interband screening effects. This study identifies a specific range of interband dielectric constants where the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) is maximized. At this optimal range, $T_c$ reaches 25 K within the doped antiferromagnetic insulating state of the material. This value represents a 15% increase compared to models neglecting screening and aligns closely with recent experimental findings. The theoretical peak in $T_c$ is attributed to the simultaneous optimization of the superconducting pairing amplitude and the superfluid density. Furthermore, the work offers a theoretical basis for the high $T_c$ observed in this compound despite its occurrence below the nickel spin-glass regime.

In dense stellar environments, neutron star composition is governed by various factors, including strangeness. While the exact mechanism for strangeness emergence remains debated—ranging from direct quark presence within hyperons to their formation via interactions between hadrons—the resulting reduction in incompressibility significantly alters dense matter properties. This study employs a family of equations of state grounded in the NLO chiral effective theory to examine how strangeness influences sound speed and the equation of state across varying baryon chemical potentials. We demonstrate that incorporating strangeness elevates the sound speed peak to approximately $c^2/v \approx 0.45$, implying a likely existence of compact objects with radii under $2\,\text{km}$ for masses around $1.4\,M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, we suggest that the evidence for a sound speed maximum is robust even without direct observation of strange compact stars.

This work introduces the definition and core properties of the Compass system, a new impactful stochastic quantum walk operating on the L²(Fock space). Uniquely, this model applies two operations during each iteration: a state compression immediately followed by a wave packet displacement. The distinct characteristics arising from this sequence enable the establishment of an evolution operator through the construction of a comprehensive relational algebra. This operator is named the "Compass," with its discovery necessitating a newly defined class of operators designated as "Compass." Despite the model's intricacy, we demonstrate that in the limit of extensive displacements, classical diffusion prevails across all initial states, effectively overriding any initial non-Gaussian features or displacements.

The Vertical Shear Instability (VSI) generates turbulent-like motions in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, facilitating the early settling of dust toward the midplane. While the VSI is constrained by disk aspect ratios and typically operates only when pressure falls off steeply with respect to the vertical axis, dust accumulation can trigger it even further outward. As dust grows and settles, the disk's midplane becomes opaque, causing the radiative transfer regime to shift from vertically transparent to opaque. This transition alters the disk's vertical thermal and density structures in ways that can either promote or restrict the VSI. Our three-dimensional hydrodynamics simulations demonstrate that in the midplane under high-opacity conditions caused by large, settled dust, the VSI is suppressed. Consequently, the outward migration of pebble-sized particles should naturally self-regulate at a certain size limit. Furthermore, high midplane opacities can facilitate the accumulation of even larger particles, potentially supporting the formation of planetary embryos.

Building upon the recent breakthrough in dynamic entrance methods for deep learning models, this study introduces the Global Mean Pooling (GMP) approach. Our proposal encompasses two primary innovations: first, the construction of a compact, lightweight network architecture designed to extract spatial embeddings derived from GMP; and the generation of temporal embeddings directly from raw video frames. These components are synthesized into a single unified vector for classification tasks. Extensive evaluations across three benchmark datasets—Kinetics-400, ActivityNet-3000, and MoviePilotOne—demonstrate that GMP consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art results. High-precision astrometry, such as that provided by the Gaia mission, measures celestial positions and motions with such accuracy that fundamental physics parameters can be inferred from the data. We also explore the effects of different prior knowledge regarding $\gamma$. Furthermore, we address a method for determining $\gamma$ using Gaia data that yields a result of $\gamma = 0.9999 \pm 0.0006$ (statistical only) for the first epoch ($t_0 = 2015.0$), corresponding to a precision of $6 \times 10^{-4}$.

Providing accurate and useful answers to open-domain commonsense questions is a significant challenge in conversational AI. Although current methods have advanced by utilizing knowledge-intensive semantic representations, they frequently generate answer lists lacking coherence and grounded in real-world logic. To bridge this gap, we propose a list selection approach grounded in open-world commonsense reasoning that employs coarse-to-neural reasoning combined with targeted question answering. Our coarse-to-neural framework identifies a preliminary subset of candidate responses and grounds them through semantic representations of open-domain commonsense knowledge. Subsequently, a "being careful" module filters this subset using rule-based regulatory reasoning to determine the ultimate answer. Evaluations across two datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both human studies and quantitative metrics.

We introduce StrollEd, a novel approach designed to mitigate issues caused to federated learning models by heterogeneous client data distributions. This method employs random selection to gather training samples from various sources, ensuring that aggregated datasets remain diverse. StrollEd offers a significant advantage over existing solutions for data distribution alignment because it does not require moving raw data to a central location, nor does it demand access to each source's storage, thereby preserving privacy and fitting within federated constraints while effectively reducing bias in non-iid scenarios without the overhead of physical transfers.

This study investigates whether a mandated psychological treatment program improves the well-being of those subjected to it. To examine this, it analyzes data from over 100,000 participants within Italy's criminal justice framework. While most inmates must undergo psychological evaluation and counseling, participation is not strictly compulsory; however, those who complete the course demonstrate significantly improved well-being scores compared to peers who do not finish it. Utilizing an administrative database, the research tracks individuals through multiple judicial stages, contrasting outcomes such as convictions and sentencing between two distinct groups: program completers and non-completers. The analysis reveals that mandatory attendance likely forces at least some inmates to engage with the material, thereby producing measurable positive effects. Furthermore, completers face lower conviction rates and, when found guilty, receive shorter prison terms. These benefits appear particularly pronounced for specific demographics, including women, younger inmates, and white individuals, suggesting that access to psychological support plays a crucial role in the broader criminal justice process.

Image segmentation is a critical step in the analysis of medical images, yet obtaining large amounts of pixel-level annotated data is often impractical. Specifically, the F1 score improved from a baseline of 0.745 to 0.761—a 2.15% gain—and the Dice coefficient increased from 0.828 to 0.852, representing a 2.90% improvement.

Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become highly effective across various domains, their internal mechanisms often lack human interpretability. Addressing this issue, we introduce a novel, intuitive variant called HistoNet, designed specifically to visualize and quantify the chaotic nature of atomic behavior in an ideal gas. By simulating an ideal gas with N atoms on a two-dimensional plane, we represent each atom as a node and its inter-atomic distances as edges. We evaluate the structural similarity of these evolving molecular graphs over time using the Fréchet Graph Distance (FGD). Our findings reveal that FGD increases monotonically as the number of atoms N grows, effectively serving as a metric for chaos intensity categorized as mild, moderate, or intense. Furthermore, we observe that N functions as a critical "hyperparameter" influencing system complexity. Most notably, we track individual atoms throughout the simulation to map their trajectories, demonstrating that the path of a single atom at any instant resembles a Brownian motion, thereby illustrating how microscopic randomness produces macroscopic patterns. Finally, we establish a direct correlation between N and temperature, demonstrating that higher atom counts and higher temperatures jointly drive greater chaos. All visual data and interactive simulations are available at https://histonet.github.io.

This study introduces GMLAB, a general software tool designed to compute the 95% maximum likelihood confidence interval for the mean value of mixed (unmatched) datasets. Although Davis & Davis (1954) offered computer programs for estimating standard errors using this likelihood approach, those were limited to matching datasets; consequently, we developed GMLAB to fill the gap for unmatching datasets.

The initial generation of stars within nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and in galactic centers likely included massive stars capable of evolving into compact remnants, potentially forming massive stellar-mass black hole clusters. The feeble gravity conjecture proposes that within any consistent compact extra-dimensional theory containing a scalar field, there exists a "tunnelling" charged state whose mass $M$ and charge $Q$ satisfy $Q/M \geqslant Q_{\text{ext}}$. It is demonstrated that $M(Q)$ is a convex function of $Q$, a property that becomes even more pronounced when the mass takes its minimal value for a given charge, $M_{\text{min}}(Q)$. The analysis reveals that convexity holds universally for any charged spectrum containing a "convex" charged state spectrum, a class that encompasses the charges of all known consistent T-duality invariant models. Furthermore, it is argued that T-duality invariance and other dualities generally enforce convexity on charged spectra, implying that the feeble gravity conjecture is likely consistent with dualities and improves significantly when applied to mass definitions restricted to dual-invariant frameworks.

This research examines the procurement of auxiliary services within the electricity sector, analyzing how various procurement mechanisms interact with broader market participation. However, their application often faces limitations due to the substantial computational resources required to perform the necessary numerical integrations. In both scenarios, we identify a specific radius in the feasible manifold such that the global minimum resides within this ball and the objective function remains geodesically convex throughout it.
